item.title: Morning Coffee: Hedge fund quant says he worked for less than $20k a year. UBS associates subjected to six month pay kink
item.description:
“Whatever we do, we’ll do it together <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/ex-brevan-howard-trader-sued-by-quant-who-joined-his-new-fund>”. Close colleagues in banking often say things like this to one another. The bonds of trust and comradeship are more important than commercial or employment relationships, and many people think of their career in terms of their allegiance to a small team or a single mentor rather than any larger institution.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
But however noble the sentiment, you shouldn’t mistake it for a contract. Finance is a tough and volatile world. Under pressure, people sometimes discover things about their friends – and themselves – which they might rather not have known. And even with the best will in the world, no matter how strong a friendship is, it can’t make something commercially viable if the numbers don’t add up. Some other things people say to each other in banking are “don’t let your mouth write a check that your wallet can’t cash”, and indeed “if you really want loyalty, get a dog”.
At one point, Robert Sicari and Wooyoung Hong had a really strong relationship. Sicari was a portfolio manager at hedge fund Brevan Howard, and in July 2023, Hong was hired to work for him as a quantitative developer and researcher. Hong says they spent weekends together at Sicari’s apartment.
Then, in November 2024, they were both fired by Brevan. Sicari began trading his own money, with a view to launching a fund, ThirtyPark, which was set up in October last year. Understandably, he invited his friend and junior to come along, and the fund launched.
But bootstrapping a hedge fund is difficult. Unless you’re very lucky or well-connected, there is likely to be a period of time when you’re basically managing your own money (and perhaps that of a few friends and family) in order to build the track record that allows you to market to outside investors. During this period, cash is tight; it’s not possible to pay yourselves Brevan Howard-like salaries (Hong says he got $400k a year at Brevan Howard in Hong Kong). Much like any other start-up, the founders are mainly working for the value of their future equity.
That equity seems to be the reason why ThirtyPark has ended up in the news, via a court filing <https://assets.bwbx.io/documents/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/rl3V0Jc0vVVQ/v0> with the New York State Supreme Court. Wooyoung Hong claims that the deal Sicari offered him included 30% stake in ThirtyPark, plus half of the profits on a designated set of the fund’s trades in Sicari's personal portfolio.
It’s always hard to tell exactly what went on from one side of a legal dispute, but the quotes and comments so far seem to suggest that there had been an underestimation of how much cash would be available, once administration, financing, margin and other expenses were taken into account. The two men disagreed about money (Sicari has declined to comment to date, other than to confirm ThirtyPark is no longer operating, according to Bloomberg). By the time the relationship broke down completely, Hong says that all he had received was a payment of $20,000 between December and January.
It’s a sad sounding story, the final truth of which will eventually come out in the courts. There might not be much to learn from it either – it certainly doesn’t mean that you shouldn’t trust people, or that it’s bad to start a business with your friends. It might just be worth remembering when someone says that they’re with you for better or worse, that the divorce courts are full of people who said that, and meant it, at the time.
Elsewhere, it’s a great day for a young banker when they graduate from the analyst program and become an associate. For UBS juniors in Zurich <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/ubs-cuts-zurich-junior-banker-starting-associate-pay-by-20-000-swiss-francs>, however, it’s going to be approximately 11% less joyous.
This is always a difficult one for payroll to handle, because analysts are typically promoted on the second anniversary of their starting date (or the third </news/these-are-awkward-times-for-the-citi-investment-banking-analysts-who-weren-t-promoted>, if your employer is old-fashioned or your MD thinks you’re not ready). That doesn’t usually coincide with the compensation year for the rest of the bank, so you go from “Analyst-2” to “Associate-0”, usually with a bit of a bonus. Then when everyone else starts a new comp year, you become “Associate-1” and start earning a proper bonus based on your own performance rather than being set for the whole class.
UBS previously paid associate-0s at the same rate (CHF175k) as first-year associates. They’ve cut this to CHF155k so that the gap from the analyst scale isn’t quite so huge. But really, by the time you reach this early milestone in your career, you ought to be growing out of caring too much about the basic salary.
Meanwhile …
“Corbets Capital” is named after a ski run in Wyoming, although as the discretionary equities arm of Balyasny, it is also where you would find the “core bets”. They are hiring at the moment; Noah Hornstrom has just joined from Citadel. (Financial News <https://www.businessinsider.com/quality-stocks-wall-street-ai-trade-high-rates-market-strategy-2026-10>)
Market strategists love their buzzwords, and apparently the current trend is to emphasise “quality” in stock picking. Everyone has their own definition of what “quality” means, although it mainly means “numbers go up”. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/quality-stocks-wall-street-ai-trade-high-rates-market-strategy-2026-10>)
If you’ve got eight years of experience as a corporate writer, and no ambitions for job security, Anthropic is offering $345,000 a year, presumably until the product can do the writing itself. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/anthropic-hiring-corporate-writer-job-advice-2026-10>)
JP Morgan is handing back its capital markets authorisation in Turkey – this is unlikely to be a big set of redundancies as they point out that the bank’s Istanbul branch (which continues) had not actually done any capital markets business since 2015. (Bloomberg <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/ai-dealmaking-startup-rogo-eyes-200-hires-in-europe-push-ea7ce96c?mod=homepage>)
Rogo, the “AI for bankers” startup founded by a computer scientist and two guys from JPM and Lazard, is hiring “aggressively” in Europe. It wants to hire 200 people, including researchers, bankers and compliance specialists, to help build and market its products, with the aim of “making sure bankers aren’t going to bed at 5am” but also “taking the top groups and helping them 10x their revenues.” (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/ai-dealmaking-startup-rogo-eyes-200-hires-in-europe-push-ea7ce96c?mod=homepage>)
For complicated historical reasons, it is illegal to trade futures contracts on onions in the USA. Some college students are campaigning to legalise it. (Marketwatch <https://www.marketwatch.com/story/meet-the-college-students-trying-to-reverse-an-obscure-ban-on-trading-onion-futures-16b8dc5d>)

item.title: Barclays fixed income traders are getting bigger bonuses at just the wrong time
item.description:
Barclays has reported its Q3 results and if you work in fixed income sales and trading there, it's looking painful.
Revenues in Barclays' fixed income currencies and commodities (FICC) business were down 19% year-on-year in the third quarter, making it the worse performing bank to report so far. Worse, even, than Bank of America </news/bank-of-america-fixed-income-poor-performance>, whose share price fell 6% in September when CEO Brian Moynihan flagged the faltering of FICC.
Barclays' CEO, C.S. Venkatakrishnan, said today that European rates traders did particularly badly in the third quarter and that securitisation professionals performed better. It was "disappointing," he added. The decline may explain why Barclays' rates traders like Hamza Hoummady </news/barclays-s-head-of-european-rates-trading-is-leaving> have been leaving. (Bloomberg reported yesterday that Hoummady is going to Qube).
The bad time for Barclays fixed income traders comes as the bank is planning to pivot pay away from higher salaries and in favour of performance-related bonuses. Like other non-EU banks, Barclays is now liberated from the European Union's bonus cap, which restricted bonuses to twice salaries. Barclays is now allowing itself to pay bonuses that are up to ten times salaries but is not planning to increase overall pay, implying a salary reduction </news/barclays-lower-salaries-higher-bonuses> sometime soon. That's good news if you've performed and bonuses are rising. Bad news if you haven't and they're not.
As it moves to a new pay model where bonuses account for a higher proportion of the total, Barclays is predictably spending more on bonuses. The bank said today that "performance costs" are up in the investment bank year-to-date. Barclays has also booked £55m of additional expenses in the investment bank as part of its programme to move senior bankers to proportionately higher bonuses and proportionately lower salaries. In July, it revealed that first half spending on "performance costs" (bonuses) was up 30%. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-21/stock-market-today-dow-s-p-live-updates>
Who will get these higher bonuses? Based upon Q3 performance alone, people working in equities sales and trading look like strong candidates. Barclays’ equities sales and trading revenues rose 47% year-on-year in the third quarter, driven by “prior investment in Prime Financing and Equity Derivatives”. In the first nine months of the year, they were up 74% on the same period of 2023. By comparison, Barclays' FICC revenues fell 19% in the third quarter and were up a feeble 2% over nine months compared with 2023.
Away from equities sales and trading, Barclays' ECM bankers and M&A bankers haven't done badly. But as the charts below show, they also haven't done well. Barclays has another £300m of restructuring spending coming in the fourth quarter.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-22/barclays-to-cut-5-000-jobs-as-ai-starts-creating-efficiency?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261022&utm_campaign=author_24141396>notes that the bank is planning to make 5,000 job cuts as AI generates "efficiency". These people will not be there to receive bonuses anyway. 60% of the cuts are coming from the middle and back office, but that leaves another 2,000 cuts coming from elsewhere.

item.title: The satirical memoirs of a managing director in an investment bank
item.description:
Ten days before the offsite, Tunde sent me the costed plan. The total at the bottom was forty-two thousand one hundred pounds. That was four thousand one hundred pounds over Hugo's number.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
A lesser leader would have gone to Hugo and asked for more money. I did not. I have always believed I would have made an excellent CFO. A true CFO does not increase the budget. A true CFO reallocates.
So I ran what Oliver calls a zero-based review, which I understand to mean starting from zero and working towards the Burgundy.
Then I found line fourteen.
Line fourteen was called Team Gift (biennial). I had to ask Tunde what it was. He explained that every two years, the London office gives every member of staff a small branded gift, as a thank-you. In 2022 it had been a golf umbrella. This year Priya had chosen a quarter-zip fleece with the Harcourt Lyle logo on the chest, at six pounds forty a unit. The line came to one thousand nine hundred and twenty pounds.
I cut it. Or rather, I re-phased it into the next capital cycle.
I will not pretend it was easy. I thought about the three hundred people who would not receive a fleece, and I felt the weight of it. But I also thought about the Burgundy. A fleece is something you forget about within a week, whereas a truly great wine is something you remember for the rest of your life. Twenty-two people remembering it is, if you think about it, a memory held in trust for the other three hundred.
I told Hugo about it that afternoon. Hugo listened. Then he said, "Richard, a CFO would have cut the leadership dinner."
I said, "And that, Hugo, is the difference between a CFO and a leader."
Priya asked me how she should tell the office that there would be no fleece this year. I suggested sustainability. A fleece, when you think about it, is essentially plastic. Priya wrote the email. It was one sentence long. I added our ESG commitments, a reference to Scope 3, which I took to be something to do with recycling, and sent it from my own account, so that it would carry weight.
I received eleven replies. Nine were out-of-office messages. One was from a man in compliance asking whether the reallocation had been approved by the sustainability committee, which I did not know we had. The last was from Dennis. It said: No problem Richard, I've still got the umbrella.
I thought that was a good attitude, and I forwarded it to HR as an example of resilience.
Great Work, Richard is available on Amazon in Kindle and paperback. <https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B0HL59CH2K> The author has over 10 years' experience in investment banking. Richard Ashworth-Hale is a pseudonym

item.title: Fake it till you make it: how to get a VC job
item.description:
Getting a job in Venture Capital (VC) </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-venture-capital> is tough. Really tough. Even with tens of billions of dollars under management, VC teams tend to be small, and very rarely have dedicated recruitment programs for students. That doesn’t mean they won’t hire juniors – but there might be a more imaginative way to do so.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
“Traditionally,” explained Patrick Blumenthal <https://patrickblumenthal.com/>, a Zurich-based investor with American VC firm Draper Associates, "you work in banking or consulting, maybe do an MBA, and then join a VC fund. Or you work at a startup first."
The problem is that, more often than not, those banking skills are useless to beginners. Founders in early-stage startups “come to you with an idea, but most of the time there’s no product, no revenue, nothing. You’re just betting on the founders,” Blumenthal said. “At that stage, banking experience doesn't help much.”
As such, getting into VC isn’t as simple as showing off your deck-making or model-building abilities. What distinguishes a VC, especially a junior VC, is the ability to find investments. “If you look at what a VC does, there are four different steps. The first step is sourcing,” Blumenthal explained. “You need to be able to find startups, and that’s basically what they’re hiring you for as a junior.”
His advice is to start doing that sourcing before anyone hires you. Pick three to five partners at a few firms you want to work for, study their investment histories – stages, industries, geographies – and “every week or every second week, send them an email with a startup you found and find quite interesting,” Blumenthal suggested.
“You say, ‘Look, I just saw this startup,’ or ‘I talked with them. The name is [X].’ Then you list three to five bullet points: what the company does, the team, what’s so special about them. The last bullet point should be about why you personally think this is a good startup.” Eventually, this works, according to Blumenthal. “If you send the partners an email directly every week or second week with one specific deal, a lot of them will respond and say, ‘Oh wow, please connect me with this startup. I want to talk.’ And if you do this a couple of times, they see how valuable you are.”
Usual copywriting rules apply; keep the message short, “in plain English,” Blumenthal explained. "Write it in your own words. Partners can tell straight away when something was written by AI, and they skip it."
The last step is to do that research, and just publish it. “I would start writing in public – on LinkedIn, a newsletter, Substack, a blog – because then people see you,” Blumenthal said. “If you do this entire loop for three months, you’re not asking for a job, because you’re already doing it.”
Of course, there’s always networking, Blumenthal said. It’s how he got his first role in VC, after all. “Just go out and tell everyone you want to work in venture capital, because you never know if someone knows someone who can introduce you.” Sometimes, the old ways are the best.

item.title: Ex-Barclays MD bemoans cost-cutting, says juniors unfairly blamed for resultant errors
item.description:
Barclays’ investment bank is no stranger to regulatory issues. One former managing director suggests cost-cutting may be behind the latest cause for scrutiny, and predicts juniors will take the blame.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Roger Versluys spent around 20 years as a managing director at Barclays before leaving in 2023. Writing on LinkedIn this week after the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/f3127b4f-d33a-4431-acff-021829f3aa72> reported that the Bank of England is examining whether Barclays traders misrepresented illiquid private credit loans to understate their risk, Versluys suggested the issue reflected a control failure caused by cost-cutting.
"Another example of a control failing as a result of prioritising cost cutting over everything else," he opined. "Expect no change in direction but a few suitably junior people to be thrown under the bus as a demonstration of ‘accountability’." Gerald Brawn, a former COO in the markets business until 2011, agreed that "Nothing changes!"
Versluys declined to comment for this article. The FT claimed that the Prudential Regulation Authority received a complaint from a Barclays insider about the placement of total return swaps referencing illiquid private credit loans into the trading book, where they would require less capitalisation than in the banking book. Barclays traders had hedged this with back-to-back total return swaps and argued that this rendered the positions tradable, said the FT.
Barclays' shares closed down 3.5% <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/barclays-scrutiny-pra-financial-derivatives-risk-bq3vkrwfc?eafs_enabled=false>on Monday after the FT's report came out. No wrongdoing has been established, but there have been various observations that hedged is not the same as liquid. <https://ghandley.substack.com/p/hedged-is-not-liquid?utm_source=substack&publication_id=8683043&post_id=221283636&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=8g1t6v&triedRedirect=true>
Responding to the FT's article, Barclays said: “Barclays’ treatment of Total Return Swaps is consistent with accounting and regulatory capital requirements. As we have disclosed previously, the total size of our private credit exposure is £15bn, the vast majority held in the banking book. Mark to market of loan TRSs on private credit assets contribute c.£0.3bn of the aggregate exposure, equivalent to c.£1.5bn of notional. Under capital rules, we are required to meet certain conditions to classify treatment as trading book. Those conditions were met and supported by appropriate governance internally and by external advisers.”
Versluys, meanwhile, is now head of structuring for EMEA over at Ripple Prime, the crypto firm. During his long years at Barclays, he was global head of prudential regulatory policy (for 12 years until 2015), before becoming an MD working across the structuring business, and latterly an MD working on principal structuring and investments.
Versluys' LinkedIn comment also suggested this week's reported eyebrow raise from the Bank of England was redolent of 2022, when Barclays revealed <https://www.ifre.com/people-and-markets/384849/barclays-nears-end-game-for-1bn-structured-notes-blunder>that it had accidentally sold US structured notes worth nearly $18bn more than its registration allowed. "Not that long since the note over-issuance where a control was missing leading to fines and buy-back losses," he observed.
Barclays' board said it deeply regretted the 2022 incident after it occurred. That incident cost the bank £894m before tax, including a $200m SEC penalty, and the cost of buying the notes back at their original price, plus interest. The SEC subsequently discovered that Barclays didn't have tracking in place to ensure it knew how many securities it was selling versus those it was registered to sell. Staff knew this was an issue, but it was not resolved. The SEC also found that when previous registration periods were up, Barclays staff calculated how much capacity was being carried over from the previous period, and that they got those calculations wrong.
It's not clear whether juniors were indeed thrown under a bus as a result of the 2022 over-issuance. Nor is it clear whether that happens often. Barclays didn't comment on Versluys' observations.
The bank reports its third quarter results tomorrow. It's in the process of cutting another £2bn from costs. It's also in the process of automating jobs and offshoring others to India.

item.title: The AI security specialists on $200k salaries in banks could earn 4x more by leaving
item.description:
Agentic AI jobs in banks are proliferating. Some are more important than others, but finding the right people to fill those spots is a hard task.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
One senior banking technology headhunter, speaking off-the-record told us that "agentic security is a big thing; each bank has at least five to ten openings in it." The interest goes all the way to the top; Jamie Dimon told the Wall Street Journal <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=glrthhLyJr8> this month that AI cybersecurity is "our biggest risk by far" and that companies are currently having to fend off armies of "little persistent agents that try to attack you."
The problem, the headhunter said, is that "people with those skills don't want to work internally for a bank. Their HR systems are so archaic and payment scales don't match what the market is paying." The most senior AI specialists at banks can earn a "minimum of $200k base plus bonus" but many earn less. A lead cybersecurity architect at JPMorgan can earn a salary of $185k working in Chicago, whereas Morgan Stanley is hiring agentic cybersecurity engineers in Baltimore on salaries of up to $195k.
These aren't bad salaries for banking, but given that average wages and salaries at OpenAI in London were $1.04m in 2025, </news/open-ai-outpaid-quant-trading-firms-in-london-last-year-offering-2m-per-head-including-stock>they look a bit paltry. Instead, the headhunter said these cybersecurity specialists are going into (or building) "small consulting firms claiming to be specialized with AI security." Pay in these consultancies can be as much as four times expected compensation in a bank. Internal hires, in comparison, "get paid crap."
The bigger problem, according to the headhunter, is that these consultancies "sound like BS. Nobody can control these things, even heads of AI security companies aren't sure what's happening." The expertise that banks are looking for "never lines up and, if it does, they're already working for Google or Palantir." </news/palantir-engineering-culture-2am>
This may not be a huge problem for now. Dimon noted that banks (which are heavily regulated) are "rather well protected." However, he said that the bank's external vendors (which may be subject to fewer regulations) could be "huge vulnerabilities" if they fall victim to a cyber attack. Dimon said that all banks should be implementing network segmentation and identity access management while also using "the most powerful AI models you have to look for vulnerabilities."

item.title: Three members of SocGen's top base metals team are now based at TD Securities instead
item.description:
French bank Société Générale has some particular talents. It is known for its equity derivatives prowess but this is not all. It also has a strength in base metals trading. But now some of its base metals guys have escaped.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
At least three members of the SocGen team - Thomas Stewart, Ben Dowse and another director - have moved to TD Securities in London. All arrived earlier this week.
TD Securities didn't respond to a request to comment on their arrivals; SocGen didn't respond to a request to comment on their departures.
Stewart and Dowse are big figures in the London metals market. Stewart spent 23 years trading metals at SocGen; Dowse spent 18 years there. In May, SocGen was declared "Base Metals House of the Year" at the Energy Risk Awards. <https://www.risk.net/awards/7963500/base-metals-house-of-the-year-societe-generale>Stewart appears to have collected this accolade on behalf of the bank.
Base metals traders are having a fine year in 2026. The London Metals Exchange (LME) had a record first half in terms of trading volumes and banks and funds have been building out teams. Citadel, for example, hired Ylan Adler from SPX Capital in January as part of an apparent <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-27/citadel-joins-trading-rush-into-metals-as-prices-soar-to-records>move into metals. Ben Green, the ex-Macquarie head of base metals at Bank of America, is on gardening leave and has yet to reappear. Ben Vicas, <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/base-metals-traders-move-battle-talent-intensifies-2026-07-30/> JPMorgan's London head of base metals trading also left in July and remains unaccounted for.
“Moves like this underline just how aggressively the market is currently bidding for deep, cycle‑tested metals expertise – highlighting how highly-prized credible senior LME talent is in this sphere in 2026,” said Luke Brace, head of metals at search firm Redstone Search. <https://redstonesearch.com/>

item.title: One of London's top energy traders just resurfaced in Jersey after leaving BlueCrest
item.description:
It's been a while, but Alex Watson's non-compete is over and he is back in action. The action will now be occurring in Jersey.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Writing on LinkedIn, Watson says he is now chief investment officer for Europe at Caerus Commodities, a Houston energy trading house with a focus on battery energy storage.
Watson declined to comment for this article.
Before he appeared at Caerus, Watson was a senior portfolio manager at BlueCrest, for whom he was also based in Jersey. We reported previously </news/bluecrest-hiring-traders-from-banks> that he left BlueCrest in February, although Watson says he's non-compete began in January '26. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-12/bluecrest-senior-gas-trader-analysts-depart-as-prices-whipsaw>reported in February that BlueCrest let go of both Watson and his six person team after extreme price moves "dented" their profitability.
Watson is a natural gas trader. Before being seduced by Mike Platt, he spent just over two years as head of natural gas trading at EDF Energy. Prior to that. he worked for Citi and Total Gas and Power.
David Hawkins, a gas trading strategist who worked with Watson at both BlueCrest and EDF, has joined him Caerus and is thought to be in Jersey too. Krzysztof Nowak, a former BlueCrest quant also resurfaced at Caerus in August, and is head of execution there.
It's not clear whether Watson intends to rehire the remainder of his BlueCrest gas trading team. Nor is clear whether Watson now intends to branch out into battery storage trading.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Anthropic is making bank CEOs look overpaid. Hedge funds have to decide who’s really a partner
item.description:
Although the big AI IPO deals appear to be on a slower track than anticipated, the teams at Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are still working hard. They have now reached the point of preparing a draft S-1 prospectus for Anthropic, a copy of which has fallen into the hands of the Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/anthropic-revenue-growth-ipo-accaf0f1?st=AtNeje&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink>. While the source of the document is not clear, and it might be a few rounds of “pls fix” from completion, there’s a lot of interesting stuff in there.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
There’s the astonishing revenue success of Claude, for example, and the equally jaw-dropping ongoing financing plans. There are the “risk factors” section, where someone appears to have taken the opportunity to write a dystopian science fiction novel taking up a third of the filing. But even more interestingly, there are details on the compensation of the CEO and President, Dario and Daniela Amodei.
And it turns out that their pay is … pretty good, but not outlandish. For the most recent year, they both got a base salary of $655k. Dario’s total compensation including stock options and awards was $18m and his sister was on $16.5m.
Which means that they would be doing well compared to European bankers. Only one unnamed Material Risk Taker </news/deutsche-bank-bonuses> at Deutsche Bank got between €17m and €18m last year; as far as we can tell this was the best-paid banker or trader in Europe, and quite a bit more than Deutsche’s CEO Christian Sewing (€10.5m <https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/deutsche-ceo-compensation-tops-10-million-euros-2025-2026-03-12/>). The Amodeis were also paid more than Andrea Orcel <https://www.reuters.com/markets/europe/unicredit-ceo-orcels-annual-pay-jumps-by-30-13-million-euros-2025-02-26/> of Unicredit (€13m) and only a bit less than Ana Botin <https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/santanders-botin-total-compensation-rises-346-2025-1854-mln-euros-2026-02-25/> of Santander (€18.5m) got for her role as executive chair.
Once you leave the euro area, though, the comparisons change. Sergio Ermotti <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/ubs-boss-ermottis-pay-stays-191-million-2025-2026-03-09/> of UBS, was rewarded with the equivalent of $19m last year, and Venkat <https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/barclays-boosts-ceos-pay-more-than-20-million-2026-02-10/> made $20m at Barclays. And then we get on to the Americans.
David Solomon <https://www.reuters.com/business/goldman-sachs-ceo-david-solomons-pay-rises-47-million-2026-01-23/> at Goldman Sachs led the bulge bracket, with total compensation of $47m for 2025. That was just ahead of Ted Pick <https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/morgan-stanley-ceo-ted-picks-pay-rises-45-million-2026-02-11/> at Morgan Stanley, who was awarded $45m. Jamie Dimon <https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jan/22/jp-morgan-jamie-dimon-pay> was on $43m, Jane Fraser <https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/boards-policy-regulation/citi-ceo-jane-frasers-pay-rises-42-million-2026-02-12/> on $42m and Brian Moynihan <https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/bofa-ceo-brian-moynihans-pay-rises-41-million-2026-02-13/> on $41m. Outside the bulge bracket, Rich Handler <https://www.salary.com/research/executive-compensation/richard-b-handler-executive-member-of-jefferies-financial-grp-inc> of Jefferies got $28m and John Weinberg <https://www.salary.com/research/executive-compensation/john-s-weinberg-executive-member-of-evercore-inc> of Evercore got $17.1m. And if you think that’s a lot of money, consider that Blackstone <https://finance.yahoo.com/news/blackstone-ceo-schwarzman-earns-over-043056110.html> paid Jon Gray more than $300m and Steve Schwarzmann $1.2bn (although these aren’t quite comparable as they include carried interest and dividends).
This isn’t necessarily to say that investment banking CEOs are paid too much, or that AI frontier lab founders aren’t paid enough. We suspect that the Amodeis will do all right in the long term. But it is slightly amusing, given everything that’s been said about the existential risk of AGI, that managing the risk of total human extinction pays almost exactly half as well as managing the risk of a bulge bracket balance sheet.
Elsewhere, the title “partner” has been no more resistant to the industry’s appetite for grade inflation than “Director” or “Managing Director”. </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> Law and professional services firms, as well as hedge funds, tend to proliferate titles like “senior income partner <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/kirkland-elliss-up-or-out-culture-is-getting-more-complicated-9c062f2b?mod=homepage>”, “salaried partner” and the like. The rule of thumb is that the more adjectives there are in the title, the further you are from actually being a partner.
Up until recently, one benefit to doing so, in London at least, was that partners, unlike employees, don’t pay National Insurance (the UK’s equivalent to Social Security contributions). However, after Bluecrest lost a case <https://www.ft.com/content/a9c9faad-7fd3-434c-99fa-7569f4a35e81?syn-25a6b1a6=1> against the tax authorities last year, the rules relating to this loophole have been clarified. Basically, sharing in the profits of the partnership isn’t good enough – you have to be someone who has “genuine influence” over the direction of its business.
This is obviously more difficult to establish the larger the firm is. So it seems that some law firms, consultancies and hedge funds are going to need to remove people from the partnership and turn them back into employees. In most cases, they will still keep their profit shares, and are likely to “remain a partner for external purposes”. But even so, it’s going to be pretty painful to be given the brutal truth.
Meanwhile …
The inside story of the power struggle at Macquarie Capital that saw Tom Butcher leave last week as Michael Milne and John Farnik were promoted. Apparently there were “disputes over credit for transactions, senior figures intervening in mandates” and a perception that the “old guard” would “cause problems” for anyone who got in their way. (AFR <https://www.afr.com/companies/financial-services/something-has-gone-awry-at-macquarie-capital-and-its-bankers-know-it-20261020-p615ww>)
David Sambur and Antoine Munfakh of Apollo have written an open letter to junior investment bankers (“Prospective Apollo Associate Candidates, Class of 2028”) telling them that Apollo will only be recruiting them after a year’s experience, rather than immediately on starting their Wall Street jobs. They are cancelling “on-cycle recruiting” for a second year and expressing hope that the rest of the private equity industry will do the same thing. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/apollo-delaying-on-cycle-recruiting-private-equity-2026-10>)
“It’s little things like that I have seen over time … it makes me grouchy and undermines my confidence about whether the GPs really have our interests at heart”. Monte Tarbox, CIO of the New York City pension fund system, was not pleased when a private equity firm tried to ask him to pay for private jet flights. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/97643fcb-46f8-43dc-b559-c33709f37866?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Despite tough conditions for hedge fund launches, people still want exposure to technology trends. Jeff Wang (formerly of Sequoia) has a track record rather than a really convincing blog post, so his Augnition Global Investors fund has been one of the few to raise more than $1bn this year. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-20/sequoia-alumnus-raises-more-than-1-billion-for-tech-hedge-fund?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261020&utm_campaign=author_1707910>)
“Scion” sounds so much more dignified than “nepo”. Profiles of Evercore’s John Weinberg and Perella Weinberg’s Peter Weinberg, grandsons of iconic former Goldman Sachs leader Sidney. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/7f771da3-0c04-4192-b2ac-4289a60fbdca?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
The European Central Bank has annual elections to its staff council. One central banker decided that it would be a good idea to run an absolutely bizarre campaign, based on the 2012 comedy film “The Dictator”. It was apparently intended to satirise restrictions on candidates’ publicity material; he has been reprimanded. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/how-a-dictator-turned-an-ecb-election-into-a-nightmare-5f400aee?mod=topic_news>)

item.title: RBC made a major systematic credit hire from BofA and now a senior guy is leaving
item.description:
Change is afoot at RBC Capital Markets in New York City. A major figure is arriving. A major figure is leaving. A business is being split into two.
RBC didn't respond to a request to comment for this article, but multiple sources say the bank has recruited Derek Hafer, the head of global macro credit trading, FICC ETF trading, and systematic trading at Bank of America. Hafer didn't respond to a request to comment.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In a memo seen by eFinancialCareers, RBC said Hafer will arrive in January as Global Head of Credit and Municipal Markets and will sit on the global markets operating committee thereafter. Various existing people (Rob Doyle, Stephen Gargiulo, Fran Lynch, Santosh Sateesh, Adam Savarese, Justin Snyder and Keith Solomon) will report to him.
While Hafer is arriving, Mark Maroney who's worked at RBC for almost 20 years and who was the bank's head of global spread products, has left. Maroney's intentions are unclear. RBC's memo from head of global markets Jonathan Hunter thanks him for his distinguished career and wishes him "all the best."
Amidst the management changes, RBC is also splitting Maroney's domain into two separate businesses - credit and municipal markets, and securitization and financing. While Hafer will run the first business, Hunter's memo says Rob Jones and Eric Wise will oversee Securitization and Financing on an interim basis. Additional new hires may follow.
Bank of America declined to comment.
Hafer is presumably planning to increase electronic trading at RBC. A new report from Crisil Coalition Greenwich says 54% of investment grade trading took place electronically in September, up six percentage points from the previous year.
Before Hafer worked for BofA, he worked for Citi, where he spent 17 years before leaving at the end of 2022. RBC likes to hire from Citi </news/citi-credit-rbc> for its credit business.

item.title: Goldman Sachs hired an AI infrastructure investment banking MD from SMBC
item.description:
The health of AI infrastructure businesses has been in question over the last few weeks, but that hasn't stopped banks from building out their AI infrastructure banking teams. </news/goldman-sachs-tmt-bankers-restructuring> Goldman Sachs just hired a senior banker from SMBC specialising in the financing arrangements for AI companies as the spotlight on firms like CoreWeave </news/brannin-mcbee> only gets brighter.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Joseph Servi joined Goldman Sachs this month as a managing director in New York for AI infrastructure investment banking with a focus on data centres, GPUs </news/trading-gpus> and fiber optics. He spent the last two years at SMBC as co-head of its asset-backed securities (ABS) </news/barclays-securitization> division as well as head of digital infrastructure and esoteric ABS origination. The role involved packaging the assets of AI infrastructure firms into securitized bonds or other products that are sold to investors. It's not clear exactly what his new role at Goldman will entail; the bank declined to comment.
Servi also previously worked in private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> as a principal with KKR working on structured capital markets for its digital infrastructure team.
Data centre ABS is a booming field; Barclays Research reported in July <https://structuredfinance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/SFA-Research-Corner_How-Data-Center-ABS-and-CMBS-Fit-in-a-Broader-Financing-Ecosystem.pdf>that outstanding issuance had grown to $61bn in 2026, up from $4bn in 2020. Some AI firms are instead using their assets as collateral for loans. CoreWeave raised $8.5bn earlier this year backed by its chips and a contract with Meta. As scrutiny of these firms increases, the need to package their financing arrangements well may become more important.

item.title: London's macro hedge fund pain as up to 100 people are out: "Everyone has blown up"
item.description:
If you're a London hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> manager covering European government bonds, these are dark days. Individual funds aren't commenting on recent performance, but headhunters and industry insiders are clear that things have not been good. "Everyone has blown up," says one senior trader at a liquidity provider, "They are all out."
The exodus of European rates traders from hedge funds comes after years of heavy hiring by London hedge funds. Traders who stayed behind in banks have been keeping a tally of how many of their often former colleagues have been spewed out again. A few weeks ago it was in the mid-70s. Now they say that closer to 100 people are out.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Both traders and headhunters say it's the end of an era. For years, hedge funds have leveraged French government bonds (OATs) in the repo market, using the bonds themselves as collateral while making money on the carry that's the difference between the yield and the cost of the repo. As French yields have risen amidst political turmoil, OATs have sold off and the whole highly leveraged trade has been upended.
"These people weren't even real portfolio managers," claims one senior trader, watching from the sidelines in a London bank. "They were just using EGBs as a carry asset. Buying bonds, sitting on the carry and getting a percentage cut. It was fun for a while. You had a lot of PMs who were long France and long Italy, but with inflation coming in and rates high, it wasn't going to last."
"Every bubble has its moment," reflects one portfolio manager in the sector.
The extent of the losses is not clear, and not everyone who has left a fund in the past month will have lost money – some departures will have other causes. But traders and headhunters say losses across the sector have been significant. "This is systemic," says one bank trader, who describes it as a "huge shock" to the hedge fund job market.
The big question now is what will become of all these unwanted hedge fund traders. Some are expected to go back to banks. "Banks need them to manage their ECB exposure and bond books," says one headhunter, speaking on condition of anonymity. The big fear now is that spreads on BTPs (Italian government bonds) will go the way of OATs, he adds.
Not all the ejected hedge fund traders will want to go back, though. And some may not be able to. Many of those now out are bound by non-competes. Some are still on guarantees </news/multistrategy-hedge-funds-pay-millions>and in no hurry to find new jobs. And in any case, banking pay doesn't compare, observes the bank trader. "These guys were all getting $1m+, but you will only get that as a desk head," he says.
It's possible that other funds will hire them. However, there are suggestions, too, that the European fixed income asset class will never be the same again. Many of the portfolio managers who blew up this month also blew up in March, says the senior trader at the liquidity provider. "They've blown up twice on the same trades." Another trader observes that a lot of funds moved into the European fixed income space in the belief that it was easy money: "The whole European carry system is now being questioned."
Some of the portfolio managers who've left have done so of their own accord, though. One says that around 10% of those who've left have gone voluntarily. "It's very hard for allocators to find people willing and able to take risk," he says. "So sometimes you have the opportunity to run your own fund with capital from others."

item.title: The definitive guide to an engineering CV in banking
item.description:
Fancy your chances of becoming an engineer at Goldman Sachs </news/2022/12/meta-tech-finance-hedge-fund-job> or another top bank? Even if you're the perfect candidate for the role, a poor first impression can get in the way of that.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Your CV </news/2023/01/banking-cv> is the first thing a banking recruiter is going to see of you, but with AI flooding the market with competent-looking CVs, how do you actually stand out?
Don't forget the basics
There’s no point curating your CV for a banking technology role if you can’t get the fundamentals right:
Save the file as a PDF. Please. Make sure your contact info and links to GitHub etc. are accurate. Keep a consistent structure when providing locations and dates for work experience and education. No photos. Pretty please. No confidential information, for your own sake. Don't overuse bold, italic or coloured text.
Don’t submit a fully AI generated resume
Everyone is using AI to assist their application process in one way or another, but giving it total control hampers your chances. Kimberly Roe, head of change and transformation IT recruitment at Huxley, told us last month </news/finance-recruiting-ai> that she receives roughly 800 CVs per day, of which three quarters have used AI to help “write the CV or… send their CV to absolutely everything.”
Fully AI-generated resumes are a faux pas. “How can we actually know anything about you?” Roe said. “It’s not your own work.” Applicants submitting CVs in this way are seen as “not legitimate.”
Roe told us that cover letters are becoming much more important because of AI-generated CVs. They were also important before; Goldman Sachs recruiters said in 2023 </news/goldman-sachs-cv-template>that they “always read cover letters… they set you apart.”
AI CVs are easy to spot, as they all describe roles and tasks in a nearly identical way. If you want to beat that, you need to understand the key frameworks yourself so you can apply your own spin.
X-Y-Z vs S-T-A-R for bullet points
Google recruiters <https://www.inc.com/bill-murphy-jr/google-recruiters-say-these-5-resume-tips-including-x-y-z-formula-will-improve-your-odds-of-getting-hired-at-google.html> suggest the X-Y-Z method for constructing your bullets. This means that you should say you "Accomplished [X], as measured by [Y], by doing [Z]." A simple and effective method for sure, but not the only one.
The S-T-A-R </news/finance/the-s-t-a-r-interview-technique>method is more commonly associated with interview processes rather than CVs. With this method, you establish a [S]ituation and define the [T]ask you were given, then expand on your course of [A]ction and the [R]esult you achieved.
Which is right for you? It depends on whether you value the result or the context more. For example, when applying for a low-latency C++ role, you might find it more important to highlight the outcome if you reduced latency by a significant degree using X-Y-Z:
Reduced tick-to-trade latency of trading systems to sub-5 microseconds by implementing lock-free queues in C++.
When providing more broad summaries of your work, S-T-A-R may be more appropriate to highlight context:
Promoted to lead engineer for tooling team, oversaw rollout of proprietary smart-pointer library used by 70% of critical systems.
Success is hard to measure in engineering, so you should choose your metrics wisely. Chip Huyen, a former Nvidia deep learning research engineer, said in a now-deleted hiring guide <https://web.archive.org/web/20240823152252/https://huyenchip.com/2023/01/24/what-we-look-for-in-a-candidate.html> that "not all [metrics which] are quantifiable are impactful” and that you should focus on the ones that delivered clear business value. Kirsty Tutton, head of technology at finance recruitment firm Selby Jennings, previously told us banks like examples of "large-scale migration" or "increasing the speed of performance."
How recruiters actually read a CV
One senior quant and technology headhunter in New York, speaking anonymously, told us that they “don’t even consider keywords” when reading a CV. Instead, the first pass of a resume “considers the person’s pedigree,” and searches for “markers of excellence.” At first glance, recruiters are more focused on where you studied, </news/best-school-for-tech-jobs-investment-banking> what prestigious firms you’ve worked for and whether you’ve received any awards.
The second pass searches for whether you have “done relevant work.” This is where most candidates fail. A senior banking technology recruiter, also speaking anonymously, said that the majority of applicants “just don’t fit the job. Maybe you could do it, but you don’t have the unique exact skills banks are looking for.”
For example, everyone knows Python, but few know PyTorch to a professional standard and fewer still have experience doing so in a highly regulated field like banking. The recruiter said that banks will occasionally make an exception and “take a chance if the candidate is young,” but there’s usually “very little leeway given.”
You also must mention the range of asset classes you've worked across; Tutton said that banks "sometimes discount CVs on the basis they are not showing particular asset class experience.” Tutton also said "banking clients like to see the tech stack used for each role as opposed to a big list."
If your role headers look like this:
Goldman Sachs Associate Python Engineer
Consider changing them to something like this:
Goldman Sachs Associate - US Equities Trading Technology Python (NumPy, Pandas) | Apache Kafka | kdb+ | Linux
Don't shorten it just for the sake of it
A one-page CV is the gold standard, short and sweet for recruiters. But just because you can cut it down to one page doesn't mean doing so will improve your odds.
Huyen said she would not reject CVs for being over one page, but strongly advises against it. “Rarely do I see a candidate whose best foot forward can't be contained within one page."
Even for those of the utmost seniority, she warns that a longer resume comes with "more chance that your biggest strengths will be buried among less important details," and that a long-winded CV without focus "shows the lack of judgement for what is important"
Can't keep your CV to a page? Try removing references, soft skills and indentation. A well-chosen font can make a significant difference also, but make sure whatever you pick is easy to read.
An example of a well optimized CV comes from Goldman Sachs’ recruitment team in 2023. </news/goldman-sachs-cv-template>
Be honest about your "expertise"
Banking is a career all about progression and growth. You will be provided the opportunity to improve your skills, but you must be honest about which skills you're actually an expert in, and which you've only got a bit of knowledge
An easy way of being honest, suggested by Tutton, is "offering a ranking out of five in order of skills within specific languages."
Honesty is important beyond just technical expertise. Leadership roles, for example, vary from title to title and Tutton says it's important to specify if your role was in 'people management' or a 'product lead.' Furthermore, job titles can also mean very different things from one industry to another (Vice President being a particularly egrigious example) so being honest about your responsibilities in a role helps clear up confusion.

item.title: The definitive guide to an engineering CV in banking
item.description:
Fancy your chances of becoming an engineer at Goldman Sachs </news/2022/12/meta-tech-finance-hedge-fund-job> or another top bank? Even if you're the perfect candidate for the role, a poor first impression can get in the way of that.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Your CV </news/2023/01/banking-cv> is the first thing a banking recruiter is going to see of you, but with AI flooding the market with competent-looking CVs, how do you actually stand out?
Don't forget the basics
There’s no point curating your CV for a banking technology role if you can’t get the fundamentals right:
Save the file as a PDF. Please. Make sure your contact info and links to GitHub etc. are accurate. Keep a consistent structure when providing locations and dates for work experience and education. No photos. Pretty please. No confidential information, for your own sake. Don't overuse bold, italic or coloured text.
Don’t submit a fully AI generated resume
Everyone is using AI to assist their application process in one way or another, but giving it total control hampers your chances. Kimberly Roe, head of change and transformation IT recruitment at Huxley, told us last month </news/finance-recruiting-ai> that she receives roughly 800 CVs per day, of which three quarters have used AI to help “write the CV or… send their CV to absolutely everything.”
Fully AI-generated resumes are a faux pas. “How can we actually know anything about you?” Roe said. “It’s not your own work.” Applicants submitting CVs in this way are seen as “not legitimate.”
Roe told us that cover letters are becoming much more important because of AI-generated CVs. They were also important before; Goldman Sachs recruiters said in 2023 </news/goldman-sachs-cv-template>that they “always read cover letters… they set you apart.”
AI CVs are easy to spot, as they all describe roles and tasks in a nearly identical way. If you want to beat that, you need to understand the key frameworks yourself so you can apply your own spin.
X-Y-Z vs S-T-A-R for bullet points
Google recruiters <https://www.inc.com/bill-murphy-jr/google-recruiters-say-these-5-resume-tips-including-x-y-z-formula-will-improve-your-odds-of-getting-hired-at-google.html> suggest the X-Y-Z method for constructing your bullets. This means that you should say you "Accomplished [X], as measured by [Y], by doing [Z]." A simple and effective method for sure, but not the only one.
The S-T-A-R </news/finance/the-s-t-a-r-interview-technique>method is more commonly associated with interview processes rather than CVs. With this method, you establish a [S]ituation and define the [T]ask you were given, then expand on your course of [A]ction and the [R]esult you achieved.
Which is right for you? It depends on whether you value the result or the context more. For example, when applying for a low-latency C++ role, you might find it more important to highlight the outcome if you reduced latency by a significant degree using X-Y-Z:
Reduced tick-to-trade latency of trading systems to sub-5 microseconds by implementing lock-free queues in C++.
When providing more broad summaries of your work, S-T-A-R may be more appropriate to highlight context:
Promoted to lead engineer for tooling team, oversaw rollout of proprietary smart-pointer library used by 70% of critical systems.
Success is hard to measure in engineering, so you should choose your metrics wisely. item.title: BNP Paribas's co-head of EMEA high yield trading is not there
item.description:
Where is Daniel Cohen, the co-head of EMEA high yield trading at BNP Paribas in London? Not, it seems, on the desk. Cohen is absent from the Bloomberg terminal. Multiple sources suggest he left last Thursday.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Cohen didn't respond to requests to comment on his whereabouts. BNP declined to comment.
High yield traders are having a hard time </news/london-s-high-yield-traders-are-suffering-after-virgin-media-left-them-exposed>as spreads blow out. BNP Paribas is also having a hard time as the French riots take their toll in its share price, which is down 15% this month. It's not clear whether Cohen's departure is related.
We understand that BNP Paribas is currently undertaking its annual appraisals and that job cuts may be coming soon. The French bank reports its results next Wednesday.
Cohen joined BNP Paribas from Jefferies in August 2024. </news/bnp-paribas-hired-a-new-head-of-high-yield-trading-even-though-it-already-has-one>BNP already employed Alun Sheppard, the former head of EMEA high yield trading at JPMorgan. Sheppard is still there.

item.title: Citadel hired Deutsche Bank's ex-Citi big US rates guy
item.description:
Pedro Goldbaum </news/pedro-goldbaum-deutsche-bank>was a big shiny deal when he arrived at Deutsche Bank in New York from Citi in London in 2024. But now Pedro has taken his golden self elsewhere.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Writing on LinkedIn, he says he's joined Citadel. Deutsche Bank declined to comment and Citadel didn't respond, but FINRA shows Goldbaum leaving DB in late September.
It was a brief stay. Goldbaum was hired by Deutsche as, “Head of Dollar Non-Linear Rates and Inflation Trading and Head of Latam Rates Trading,” as part of the German bank's push into US fixed income trading. How's that going? We will know when Deutsche reports its third quarter results next week.
Goldbaum is a Citi guy at heart. He spent nearly 12 years there before leaving in October 2023 and was Citi's co-head of global rates. The Deutsche Bank job title always looked a bit less shiny than that. Now Goldbaum will be illuminating at Citadel instead.

item.title: Hedge fund Schonfeld shows which hedge fund jobs are proliferating. It's bus dev
item.description:
Schonfeld, the hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, has filed some UK accounts for Schonfeld Strategic Advisors LLP and if you're interested in knowing who they've been hiring at a high level, you will be fulfilled.
Unlike other hedge funds with UK accounts, Schonfeld helpfully breaks down its headcount by function. Since 2022, it has increased its London headcount by 71 people. But some functions have benefitted from proportionately more hiring than others.
As the chart below shows, the function that's grown most during this period is business development </news/hedge-fund-business-development-executive-bde>, which is the exalted hedge fund term for recruiters who hire portfolio managers. Business development professionals are not just recruiters, though. As the head of bus dev at Point72 observed recently <https://pitchthepm.substack.com/p/why-point72-wins-20-years-next-to?utm_source=substack&publication_id=7758668&post_id=217182070&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>, they also see themselves as doing an investing role. It's just that they're investing in portfolio managers, who then invest for the fund.
At the end of 2025, Schonfeld had 20 people working in bus dev in London, up from only six in 2022. This year, it's lost at least one of them - Sameer Buch </news/hedge-fund-millennium-hired-hedge-fund-schonfeld-s-top-equities-recruiter-in-london>- to Millennium.
Schonfeld's London bus devs have then been accumulating London portfolio managers. A net nine PMs were added last year. 25 have been added since 2022. By comparison, trading, risk and standard HR roles have dwindled.
Despite Schonfeld's portfolio manager hiring in 2025, the FCA Register suggests that five investment professionals left in September (Rastko Miletic, Joseph Bond, both PMs, and Andrew Prentice, Peter Hunt and Sourabh Tripathi). Their departures are thought to follow Manus Baveja's exit to Dymon in August.

item.title: Morning Coffee: 'Dignified' but unexpected pre-Christmas banking job cuts are go. Another accidental email was sent
item.description:
It's Q4, which means that 'tis the season of banking job cuts. The first to shake out the seasonal ornaments is National Australia Bank (NAB), which yesterday made an apparently unexpected post <https://www.nab.com.au/news/nab-updates/nab-simplifying-operating-model-and-alignment-to-customer-priorities>saying that it will be making 2,500 roles or 6% of its staff redundant, of whom 1,500 will go before Christmas.
All these people will be treated with "dignity and respect", said NAB. They will be engaged and consulted with, redeployed and reskilled and given support in their "transition." They will also be given redundancy entitlements according to "applicable industrial instruments," which sounds complicated.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
NAB's cuts aren't really that surprising. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/nab-to-cut-2-500-staff-use-fewer-consultants-and-contractors>notes that NAB already made cuts in its investment bank in August <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-21/australia-s-nab-cuts-banker-jobs-in-institutional-division>, when it combined origination and sales roles and said, "We recognise change can be difficult."
For bankers and traders and bank employees in locations beyond Australia, NAB's new cuts may not seem relevant. But they are the zeitgeist. NAB is cutting to "improve outcomes for customers by reducing duplication and speeding up decision making." It is focusing on "reducing the size of corporate functions. It is "simplifying its operating model." And it's trying to "better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives."
Bloomberg suggests NAB's doing this now because things aren't great in the Australian housing market, where a severe property downturn has weakened demand for NAB's mortgages. Australia is not alone in this. <https://www.fca.org.uk/data/mortgage-lending-statistics>And NAB is not alone in wanting to be a sleeker place with technologically empowered humans who can handle hard change. HSBC, Citi, Standard Chartered, Barclays and others have similar intentions.
Separately, watch what you send by email.
Following the email error at Morgan Stanley </news/morgan-stanley-md-email>, in which MD Mohamed Atmani </news/mohamed-atmani-morgan-stanley> accidentally sent a list of proposed deals and some prices to clients, the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/6075e0ec-9116-4de4-84e6-d50b5ed1d47a?accessToken=zwAAAaFUlDTRkc9gdeDskRZN5NOE5tULXtHUeg.MEUCIQDJ1Mj9bVt_d87G8QF5R0OOX5mtK2RNbVtzLQnpJALHkQIgMXemN_Gm_vbJJQfVZPFZEnYZGwfkfTJd-15i-5HrpsE&segmentId=e95a9ae7-622c-6235-5f87-51e412b47e97&shareId=b4e48217-ec88-4b13-8f0a-d3a55c42ee90&shareType=enterprise&syn-25a6b1a6=1> reports that another accidental email was sent by the most senior people at law firm Freshfields.
The Freshfields email concerned an exchange between the firm's global managing partner Alan Mason and its co-head of US corporate and M&A, Ethan Klingsberg. The two men were discussing how they might spin out Freshfields' legal AI unit and Klingsberg suggested they might try “sophisticated investors that are respected by the rest of the investor community for their leadership”, and then added that this “probably” ruled out “Middle Eastern sovereign wealth money”.
The FT says Mason then accidentally emailed the exchange to a large internal distribution list, some of whom took screenshots.
“We apologise unreservedly for a comment made about Middle Eastern sovereign wealth investors . . . the comment does not reflect the position or beliefs of the firm or those participating in that email exchange, and we sincerely regret the offence caused,” Freshfields said in a statement made to the FT on Monday. It added: “We hold our clients across the Middle East in the highest regard and deeply value the longstanding relationships and trust we have built in the region. We have enormous respect for the discerning leadership and global impact of our clients and remain firmly committed to the region.”
Meanwhile...
Finance is full of jobs that are made up of well-documented, routine tasks where completion can be easily tracked. For banks and insurers, these might include roles handling queries from customers or other staff, overseeing approvals for risk, or monitoring technology and operations. Finance also has the highest share of occupations exposed to AI of any industry at 84%, according to the Bank of England. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-opinion-how-will-ai-affect-jobs-the-uk-finance-industry-is-showing-us/?taid=6ad59ba393db840001f32534&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Optiver wants $900m in financing to expand its trading activities. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/high-frequency-trader-optiver-seeks-900-million-debt-package>
Private equity firms have started trying to expense private jets. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/97643fcb-46f8-43dc-b559-c33709f37866?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Barclays traders discovered that it can put total return swaps referencing illiquid private credit loans in the trading book if they make them into a traded position using a matching trade with another counterparty (known as a back-to-back total return swap). It becomes a traded position even though the loan referenced is illiquid. The regulator is not so sure. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/f3127b4f-d33a-4431-acff-021829f3aa72?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Seth Platt is leaving Two Sigma and co-founder David Siegel must now pick his third proxy on the management committee in about two years amidst his dispute with John Overdeck. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/two-sigma-to-lose-top-executive-seth-platt-amid-founders-feud?taid=6ad67ca2f1222300014cf14e&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
The dispute between Overdeck (who runs quants at Two Sigma) and Siegel (who runs the engineers building the trading systems) highlights the difference between the two jobs. “I would liken the trading and modeling to the striker, or the guy who kicks the ball in the goal at the end of the play,” said Overdeck. “Investment management is very much a team sport. I was managing the very offensive end of the field." (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/two-sigma-overdeck-divorce-siegel-d66db008>
HireVue type interviews are susceptible to fraud and interviewees are being asked to do weird things like hold up fingers and provide proof of identity. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/16e1d29b-3680-4712-b8e7-ed4a4125041a?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
HSBC's departing CFO Pam Kaur has worked for 12 CEO's during her career and thinks the speed of changes at HSBC is manageable. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/hsbcs-first-female-cfo-pam-kaur-on-40-years-in-finance-stepping-down-and-sewing-her-own-gowns-02a8038c>
Now is your chance to be head of asset management at HSBC. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/hsbc-starts-search-to-replace-asset-management-head-moreau?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261019&utm_campaign=author_20887312>

item.title: London's high yield traders are suffering after Virgin Media left them exposed
item.description:
Working in high yield trading can be a very lucrative business. It can also be a very painful one.
Following this month's descent of Virgin Media O2's bonds into distressed territory, multiple sources say that some banks' European high yield trading desks are nursing large losses.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The banks concerned either didn't respond or declined to comment.
Virgin Media O2's bonds plummeted in early October after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said provisionally that a plan involving Virgin Media joint venture Nexfibre Networks to acquire Netomnia Ltd, could lead to reduced competition in the UK broadband market.
If the Nexfibre-Netomnia deal goes through, Virgin Media will get £1bn of cash to help pay down its roughly £22bn of debt. The CMA is due to make its final ruling on the deal December 15th. In the meantime, Virgin Media's debt is in distressed territory and high yield desks and hedge funds holding the debt are thought to be nursing large losses. If the CMA decides the deal can go ahead, these losses could yet be recovered.
Desks understood to have lost money recently on the so-called "VMED trade" include JPMorgan's high yield desk in Europe; JPMorgan declined to comment. Separately, a senior high yield trader has also left another London bank in recent weeks, according to people familiar with the matter. The reason for his departure is unclear.
High yield desks have made large profits for successful traders in the past. However, JPMorgan’s European high yield business has also seen multiple senior exits in recent years. They include Bhavit Sawjani, whose team at ExodusPoint reportedly lost more than $70m </news/bhavit-sawjani-jpmorgan-hedge-fund> after he left the bank, and Gianfranco Canepa, whose former team at JPMorgan built up a €500m position </news/2022/12/jpmorgan-high-yield-loss> in French grocer Casino Guichard-Perrachon and also bet on Metalcorp, a subsidiary of Monaco Resources Group. Those positions reportedly swung to a loss of nearly $70m after Canepa left.

item.title: Balyasny reshuffled its applied AI team after its head of research moved into trading
item.description:
Even if you're working on cutting edge applied AI in a hedge fund, </news/how-hedge-funds-use-ai> you're not technically front office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking>. That doesn't mean you can't make the switch, as one of Balyasny's most senior researchers just proved.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Peter Anderson </news/balyasny-hedge-fund-generative-ai-google>, who was most recently head of research for applied AI at the fund, has now become head of autonomous strategies within its fundamental equities. Anderson joined Balyasny from Google, but briefly worked as a graduate equity researcher </news/i-spent-30-years-in-equity-research-the-job-only-got-harder> for Credit Suisse before going back to school for a machine learning PhD.
Autonomous strategies in a fundamental team seems somewhat oxymoronic. Balyasny didn't respond to a request for comment, but Anderson's role may be focused on taking the fundamental research of Balyasny's equities researchers and translating it into trading algorithms. </news/2023/03/python-algorithmic-trading> The fund has a separate systematic trading division run by Francine Fang.
Balyasny's chief AI officer Charlie Flanagan is also a Google alum and has filled Anderson's role with one more Googler. Balyasny's new head of research is San Francisco-based Gearoid Murphy who was a senior researcher in the tech firm's innovation lab, X (not the app). He most recently was CTO of a project focused on using AI "to reduce waste, fragility, and inefficiency in the global supply chain." Murphy has a PhD in 'evolutionary algorithms' and also worked in the video game industry </news/the-video-game-that-will-prove-you-deserve-a-job-in-commodities-trading>with physics engine provider Havok.
The fund also hired Itamar Kestenbaum in New York. He joined a senior AI engineer and was most recently a senior engineer in the infrastructure team at Meta in New Jersey. Before that, he spent several years working across tech firms in Israel.

item.title: Jane Street employees all have an AI twin that does their knitting for them
item.description:
Investment banks are building digital employees. </news/jpmorgan-bankers-ai>Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>is building 'AI Users.' The big difference is that these users uniquely correspond to each human employee at trading firm. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Speaking on the Signals and Threads <https://signalsandthreads.com/the-changing-craft-of-programming/#whats-left-of-the-craft-011514> podcast over the weekend, Jane Street engineer John Crepezzi said that the firm has built identities through which AI agents </news/how-ai-is-affecting-careers-in-electronic-trading-and-hft> can act, "which are alternate versions of each of the people at the firm." Jane Street engineers code through Claude Code, Codex, or Jane Street's internal coding systems.
This was initially just a security classification so that Jane Street's systems would "apply the right set of rules" when an agent was acting on your behalf "because they know that the caller is an AI version of you." Since then, however, Crepezzi said that the firm has "built other systems that take use of this AI-concept."
One new use case is a code tracking system that monitors what code was written by these AI users </news/developers-are-doubling-their-code-output-with-ai-is-that-a-bad-thing> and what was written by a human. Crepezzi didn't mention other use cases, but said the AI user structure is "show[ing] up in a bunch of other places too."
One of the ways that these users are called into action is through Jane Street's internal slack. Agents will start a project when prompted via chat and start writing the code for it without having to be prompted. Crepezzi said that "something like 45% of the total released features" start in this manner.
How is AI changing Jane Street
We've written about how AI is changing Jane Street's famous internships </news/what-interns-at-jane-street-actually-do-from-2022-to-now>. CTO Ron Minsky has said in the past that there's increased focus on reviewing code rather than writing it due to the tendency of AI to write "uncanny" programs </news/jane-street-cto-everyone-knows-python-lots-of-people-aren-t-any-good-at-it#:~:text=It%27s%20not%20just,still%20super%20broken.%22>that look functional but are "super broken." Senior employees are coding less too, but they're not necessarily happy about it.
Speaking on the most recent podcast, Minsky likened coding to "knitting... you're not maybe solving any big ideas, but the craft of putting the code together" is an "artistic" pursuit. Crepezzi said that the focus is now more on "watching the code that it wrote and offering adjustments where you can."
There are benefits too. Crepezzi noted that AI users starting pull requests through Slack saves you from "a lot of toil involved in just creating a new pull request." Minsky said it also gives engineers time to work on the "code that you would’ve never bothered to write at all."
Crepezzi noted that systems design (the big picture stuff) is "still fairly protected." Minsky suggested that it has also become the bulk of work for Jane Street engineers; he was told by a "very strong engineer" that their work was previously 10% "thinking really hard and deeply about what to do," then 90% executing - now, Minsky said that engineer will offload the execution to an LLM and do "another one of those 10%" problems.

item.title: Barclays head of European rates trading is leaving
item.description:
Hamza Hoummady, the head of European rates trading at Barclays, is understood to be leaving the bank.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Barclays declined to comment and Hoummady didn't respond to a request to comment. Multiple sources say he has resigned. His destination is unclear but he's not thought to be joining a rival bank. There are unconfirmed suggestions that he might be working on a new venture involving data centres.
Hoummady rejoined Barclays from Goldman Sachs in 2022. He previously spent 11 years at the British bank before leaving for Goldman in 2018 and was a popular figure there.
Barclays insiders are lamenting Hoummady's disappearance. It comes after the departure of numerous other members of the macro team, including - most recently James Hackett </news/another-rates-md-left-barclays-in-london-after-resigning-earlier-this-week>, an MD in sales - for a destination that remains unknown.
It's conceivable that Hoummady is joining a fund. London macro funds have ejected quantities of portfolio managers after a troublesome time in 2026, and have seats to fill.
It's not clear who will do Hoummady's job at Barclays. Punitha Raja </news/punitha-raja-barclays> is flavour of the year, but is in sales and is only a director. Guy Winkworth is a possibility. Mark 'The Whale' Wade joined </news/barclays-hired-the-whale-from-nomura> recently, but is comparatively junior. Or Barclays could hire one of the many macro traders to have left a fund in recent months. There's plenty of choice, including the array of senior people who've left BlueCrest. </news/leaving-bluecrest-macro>

item.title: Ex-Citi trader out at hedge fund Capula appears to be leaving after three months
item.description:
It is a bad year to work in a macro hedge fund in Europe. European government bond traders from banks who tried their hands at macro trading in funds are disappearing from their new seats. They are thought to include one former Citi trader who only - finally - joined a hedge fund in the summer.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Multiple sources say that Michele Beretta, </news/capula-hedge-fund-hiring> a former European government bond trader at Citi in Paris, who joined Capula Investment Management a few months ago, is leaving again. The FCA Register shows Beretta arriving in July and exiting the London entity on October 15th. He's still thought to be employed there for the moment.
Beretta didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Capula declined to comment.
Beretta joined a pod at Capula that was run by Andrea Casulli, an ex-Goldman Sachs and UBS rates trader. The FCA Register shows Casulli himself leaving at the end of July 2026.
In the year ending March 2025, Capula's London hedge fund partners were paid </news/capula-hedge-fund>an average of £7.8m each, down from £10.5m in 2024. The average employee there earned £435k last year.
