item.title: Goldman Sachs euphemistically explained yesterday why banking careers aren't what they used to be
item.description:
Goldman Sachs is having a great time. In yesterday's investor call, CEO David Solomon </news/david-solomon-goldman-sachs> explained that "we're in a top quartile environment" and pointed out that he had said so three times. "Capital markets activities are strong," Solomon said, while acknowledging that the macro situation is "a little bit more complicated."
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In these top quartile times, it might be expected that Goldman Sachs would be hiring and paying. To some extent, this is true. Once again, </news/banking-jobs-2026> though, there's a disconnect between the times for banks and the times for their employees.
Speaking yesterday, Denis Coleman, Goldman's CFO, explained that Goldman is focused on growing its revenues, while reducing the proportion of those revenues that it spends on compensating employees.
"As we look at ways that we can invest to grow the firm, grow the earnings of the firm, scale the firm, we are building durable platform-connected types of businesses," said Coleman. "And over time, we should not have the same degree of headcount-related expenses that we might have historically to grow and scale the firm."
In Goldman parlance, 'platform-connected' businesses are businesses that allow revenues to increase rapidly without having to add extra people. These businesses include the financing businesses that sit in prime services </news/prime-broking>, said Coleman. Equities financing revenues at the firm rose 96% year-on-year <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-13/goldman-s-equity-traders-take-back-seat-to-prime-brokerage-arm> in the third quarter, but this was mostly thanks to "the firm's financial resources and risk appetite," Coleman explained.
The subtext is that Goldman has not had to hire new people to grow. In the year to the end of September, headcount at the firm fell by 800 people. In the third quarter, 1,300 people were added, but this included up to 2,500 new graduates and entry level hires.
For some people at Goldman, though, things are still very good. These people include David Solomon, who will receive stock worth circa $100m </news/how-to-earn-100m-at-goldman-sachs> in the next few weeks once a historic bonus vests. Pay per head for the average Goldman employee was around $350k for the first nine months of this year, up 19% on the same period of 2025.
Coleman also said that the "very, very best people" are still very much in demand and that Goldman will "compensate them appropriately." These people include "business professionals" and engineers.
At the same time, though, the emphasis is on building a business that can grow, while spending proportionately less on employees. This is why compensation spending as a proportion of revenues at Goldman was only 27.4% in the third quarter, its lowest Q3 level since 2021. It's also why the compensation ratio for the first nine months as a whole is the lowest for at least five years.
This trend will continue, said Coleman. The future is about "sustainably delivering operating leverage to our shareholders." It's not about hiring a lot of expensive new people.

item.title: Morning Coffee: JPMorgan's enormous pay package enticed BofA's special banker. The trader who beats the Street from a garage
item.description:
As the advertising guru Bill Bernbach once said, “a principle isn’t a principle until it’s cost you money <https://www.reesehopper.com/blog/its-not-a-principle-until-it-costs-you-money>”. It’s a proverb that the human resources departments of many investment banks will recognise. Setting sensible policies with respect to compensation, promotion and even compliance is one thing, but enforcing those policies when they risk losing an important hiring battle is another.
Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/world/bank-america-loses-bankers-tells-staff-big-ambition-continued-hiring-2026-10-13/> suggests Bank of America <https://www.reuters.com/world/bank-america-loses-bankers-tells-staff-big-ambition-continued-hiring-2026-10-13/> is sticking to its principle. Despite increasing its ambition in investment banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> and steadily hiring over the last few years, BoA has for the most part kept to a bonus structure </news/2021/01/bank-of-america-bonuses-vesting> which emphasises deferred compensation and equity grants over immediate payouts. According to European regulatory disclosures </news/salaries-and-bonuses-goldman-sachs-jpmorgan-citi-baml-morgan-stanley>, its Material Risk Takers (the highest paid staff) only got 20% of their last bonus in non-deferred cash, compared to an average for the rest of the bulge bracket closer to 40%.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This is good news for shareholders and management, as it should mean that BoA rainmakers are more likely to be locked in and harder to poach. As long as the share price keeps going up (like it has for the last two years), it’s pretty good news for employees too. But, it does make things a little difficult for bankers who have mortgages and college tuition to pay (or, indeed, expensive watches and yachts to buy). And many bankers just like to be paid in immediate cash; lots of things can happen in this industry, and another proverb holds that “a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush”.
According to some employees quoted by Reuters, the BoA compensation structure may have been a factor in some high-profile departures, like those of Kevin Brunner, David Fishman or Mike Joo. It hasn’t stopped them from hiring other rainmakers (like Jason Rowe, George Murphy and Alban de la Sablière), but apparently the overall recruitment position was sufficiently unsettling for Faiz Ahmad, the head of global investment banking, to hold a town-hall meeting with 50 top bankers in order to reassure everyone that the bank hadn’t lost its ambition. As the company told Reuters, “We have strong momentum across our global business … We have recruited dozens of senior bankers this year from our major competitors”.
The loss of BofA's particularly special banker, Amy Lissauer, to JP Morgan appears to have hit particularly hard. Her activist defence team was something of a crown jewel <https://www.ft.com/content/62b70b3a-88c9-4d6c-bc0c-b840586af91a?syn-25a6b1a6=1> for BoA, and JPM certainly didn’t lose any time in sending out a press release to boast about hiring her. The fact that she left in the same week that Mike Joo resigned as co-head of investment banking must have made it hit somewhat harder. And it’s always disquieting when an employer has clearly tried their hardest to match a competitor’s offer, but been unable to stretch quite as far.
On the other hand, these things are always happening in investment banking; industry churn is what keeps the market honest. We wouldn’t expect Bank of America to change their pay philosophy, and it might even be a bad sign if they did. Although Bill Bernbach didn’t say this, giving up on a principle usually costs you more money in the long term.
Elsewhere, you would normally think that in order to be a profitable macro trader, you need a Bloomberg Terminal, a low-latency connection and possibly a dozen economists and analysts. The high cost of establishment is one of the reasons why people join “pod shops”. However, Brian Golden <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-10-13/kalshi-s-top-inflation-trader-beats-wall-street-banks-from-his-garage> has made $2m out of inflation trading with a laptop, an Excel spreadsheet and a standing desk that he made for himself out of cinder blocks in his garage. As he says, if he was one of the many bank forecasters who he outperforms, “I would be humiliated. I would be so embarrassed”.
But Wall Street can save a little face. Golden makes his money by trading on the Kalshi prediction market for each month’s CPI release. His spreadsheet is made up of a lot of formulae which reproduce the official calculation, and which allow him to be very precise about the current month’s index. It’s not quite the same thing as trying to forecast inflation a year ahead, and to make trades in professional size on economically meaningful markets. Nevertheless, Morgan Stanley is apparently going to use Kalshi data in its own forecast model, although they aren’t yet going to be copying Golden’s spreadsheet or his desk design.
Meanwhile …
Laura Janssens, the head of investment banking at Berenberg is leaving to “take a break from the industry before pursuing other challenges”. It’s been an exhausting time at Berenberg with a lot of top management turnover; she’ll be replaced by Gunnar Regier who joined the board two weeks ago. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/berenberg-investment-banking-head-janssens-departs-after-management-overhaul-4e83a8fc?mod=topic_news>)
It seems to be a trend in the market that whenever things get really sticky, humans take market share from automated venues. The latest piece of evidence is in the euro repo market – as the Iran War made people rush for cash, voice traders’ share went up by 2.5pp. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-13/euro-repo-traders-turn-to-humans-over-machines-in-flight-to-cash>)
Employment data seems to suggest that banks are indeed cutting junior roles as a result of AI, but that this is all happening in commercial and retail banking – junior roles in investment banking and capital markets are, if anything growing faster than they were before ChatGPT came out. (Revelio <https://www.reveliolabs.com/news/ai-and-work/ai-junior-bankers-hiring-data>)
Martin Shkreli, the notorious “pharma bro” was banned for life from owning shares in the pharmaceutical industry in 2017. The regulators have recently alleged that he’s been trading them on a livestream for his YouTube channel. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/health/pharma/ftc-states-ask-court-to-hold-pharma-bro-shkreli-in-contempt-for-trading-drug-stocks-152dbc30?mod=mhp>)
The New Zealand investment banking market might be a small pond, but there’s a lot of fishing going on; after losing several staff to Barrenjoey earlier in the year, Jarden have now taken two managing directors from Forsyth Barr. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-12/jarden-hires-two-forsyth-barr-directors-in-nz-talent-battle>)
“If you’d have asked me 10 years ago the stuff that I was doing today, I’d would’ve said you’ve lost your mind.” That might be a slightly concerning quote if it came from a banker, but actually it’s from a manufacturer of deal toys, referring to the impact that AI design and 3D printing have had on the desktop kitsch industry. (Fast Company <https://www.fastcompany.com/91616835/theyre-cheap-theyre-kitschy-and-investment-bankers-love-them>)

item.title: Hedge fund Verition parted company with 5 macro traders, and hired someone new
item.description:
Verition, the friendly multistrategy hedge fund </news/2023/05/verition-hedge-fund>might be friendlier than some of its rivals, but this does not mean that everyone stays. Verition trimmed <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-26/verition-shutters-team-led-by-ex-goldman-traders-lashgari-paul> a trading run by two Goldman Sachs traders at the end of last year. It trimmed Damien Couture </news/hedge-fund-cuts-french-quant-who-battled-hard-to-work-there> in July. And now at least five other people have gone, of their own volition or not.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Verition declined to comment for this article, but multiple sources tell us that three ex-Nomura rates traders who joined in 2022 have left, as have a former Brevan Howard portfolio manager and an ex-UBS STIR trader.
The departed Nomura traders are Stanley Sun, Will Hirschmann and Grant Web. It's thought they were in a macro/relative value pod based in New York. We messaged Sun and Hirschmann for this article; neither responded.
The ex-Brevan leaver is Ken Wang, a rates and relative value trader who joined in 2024. Wang also didn't respond to a request to comment.
Meanwhile, James Regan, a former head of G11 STIR trading at UBS in London who joined Verition in 2024 and left in July 2026, has just turned up at Millennium in New York.
Verition is also thought to be in discussions with Dubai-based Antonio Belgioioso, a top Italian macro trader who joined the firm from Goldman Sachs in 2025. It's not clear whether Belgioioso also intends to leave.
While there have been departures, there have also been arrivals. In London, for example, Verition has just hired Chris Telfer, a macro credit portfolio manager from Athlone Investment Management. Verition recently expanded into Eisler Capital's empty office space and so has many seats to fill.

item.title: Wells Fargo is "immensely bullish" on AI... kind of
item.description:
Wells Fargo, </news/wells-fargo-s-engorging-technology-banking-team-hired-an-md-from-ubs>like every other bank, is in the throes of adopting AI </news/how-to-get-a-banking-ai-job> as a means to cut costs (ergo, jobs). Speaking in its Q3 earnings call, CEO Charlie Scharf said that the bank is "immensely bullish" on the latest batch of models, despite not seeing much impact from AI on the jobs market.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Scharf said the bank is "devoting significant management time and resources" to AI. Much of this is around AI coding capabilities; </news/developers-are-doubling-their-code-output-with-ai-is-that-a-bad-thing> Scharf said engineers are "using it to write code faster" and have been using agentic coding tools "where appropriate." The bank has used AI to "identify as well as write and test code" to address "cybersecurity vulnerabilities", and has used AI to "accelerate response time for underwriting decisions." With automation comes a reduction in force. The bank's results showed that headcount had fallen 8% year-on-year.
Wells Fargo's observations on the broader workforce tell a different story. CFO Mike Santomassino said that Wells Fargo's commercial bank performance was aided by the fact that "wages and employment continue to be strong" and that the bank is also "not seeing signs of that changing." The bank didn't make any mention of whether AI is positively or negatively affecting wages and employment, but Santomassino said that the strong performance was true across "all of the different cohorts of clients" the bank has in terms of income and wealth level. AI driven cuts at other banks have focused on getting rid of 'lower-value human capital </news/lower-value-human-capital>' which would suggest that lower income workers would be disproportionately affected. Perhaps not.
Maybe Wells Fargo is just built different. Scharf said that "there’s this underappreciation for the benefits that those with scale have when it comes to AI." He said that, if an agent is used to replace the work of someone in a call centre, the bank can "spend the same amount of money somewhere else but deploy it more broadly." Scharf said that the bank is "focused on building a company that has higher embedded returns."
It's not just AI that's making things faster. Santomassino said that, through tokenized payments infrastructure, payments which previously took up to two days can now be done "in two minutes or less."

item.title: Citi's M&A bankers appear to be having a hard time, especially in America
item.description:
Today is the day of Citi's Q3 results (and Goldman's Q3 results </news/prime-broking>and JPMorgan's </news/jpmorgan-q3-2026> Q3 results). Even before the results came out, though, it was clear that Citi's M&A bankers aren't exactly on fire in the same way that its equity capital markets (ECM) bankers are.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The charts below are constructed from market share data provided by data provider Dealogic. They cover the period from January through to October 7th, slightly beyond the third quarter.
Citi’s market share by year: M&A, DCM and ECMShare of volume (%), 1 Jan to 7 Oct of each year; 2026 highlighted. Bar heights use one scale per product row, so the four regions in a row can be compared.M&A · Global21.5 12.4 14.7 18.1 14.0 15.7 14.6 10.8 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26M&A · North America26.4 14.0 16.7 17.7 18.1 22.9 18.4 11.3 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26M&A · EMEA19.5 21.1 18.4 20.5 12.8 12.3 15.0 14.6 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26M&A · APAC ex Japan7.9 2.5 14.7 14.7 8.4 6.7 4.8 8.6 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26DCM · Global6.0 6.2 5.9 5.5 5.0 5.6 5.4 5.0 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26DCM · North America9.2 8.5 8.0 8.4 7.4 8.0 7.7 6.9 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26DCM · EMEA5.7 5.6 5.6 4.9 4.8 5.5 5.2 4.9 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26DCM · APAC ex Japan1.8 2.5 2.2 1.6 1.5 1.4 1.1 1.3 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26ECM · Global6.1 6.9 6.5 4.5 4.3 6.3 4.6 6.3 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26ECM · North America7.8 8.8 7.4 6.4 4.9 6.0 4.1 6.7 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26ECM · EMEA6.4 7.8 6.5 6.8 6.5 5.3 6.5 4.8 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26ECM · APAC ex Japan3.9 4.3 5.8 2.6 2.8 8.8 4.4 7.0 ’19’20’21’22’23’24’25’26Source: Dealogic, data to 7 October 2026. M&A gives full credit to every adviser on a deal, so shares overlap and are not comparable with DCM/ECM, where credit is split between bookrunners.
As the charts show, Citi's ECM bankers are mostly thriving, especially in North America. But Citi's M&A bankers are mostly not thriving, especially in North America.
What has gone wrong? Citi declined to comment on the charts above. Its third quarter results today showed global M&A revenues falling 4% year-on-year in the third quarter, even while M&A revenues at JPMorgan were up 32% and M&A revenues at Goldman were up 18%. Citi's ECM revenues, however, were up 77%.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-06/citi-takes-top-spot-in-global-ipo-underwriting-through-september>reported last week that Citi is the top IPO underwriter globally this year. It probably helps that Citi's investment bank is being run by people </news/citi-paid-vis-raghavan-25m-to-hire-from-jp-morgan-jp-morgan-paid-doug-petno-23m-to-hire-from-citi>with an ECM background. The reason for its M&A lassitude is less clear. The US bank said today simply that revenues were down "amid a lower wallet". This might imply that Citi lacks strength in key sectors, like tech. </news/highest-paid-bankers>However, as we've observed previously, Citi's historically strong sectors </news/citi-m-a> have included tech but also energy, industrials and natural resources.
This isn't the first time Citi's M&A weakness has been on display. The bank's issues were equally visible after the first half. At that time, we noted </news/citi-m-and-a>that the bank had said it was still understaffed and that it's busy hiring - particularly in healthcare, industrials, technology and sponsors; but it takes a while for all the new bankers to bed in.
In North America, in particular, Citi has added a new co-head of North America investment banking in the form of David Friedland, an ex-Goldman Sachs partner, who arrived in January. Friedland has recently been making pronouncements </news/these-are-awkward-times-for-the-citi-investment-banking-analysts-who-weren-t-promoted> about Citi's top junior talent and appears to have been instrumental in shortening Citi's analyst program </news/now-citi-will-promote-even-its-moderately-good-analysts-to-associate-after-two-years>to help retain people. Working on more deals might help with that, too.

item.title: JPMorgan increased pay in its investment bank. Here's who should get it
item.description:
Q3 reporting season has begun. As usual, the American bulge brackets are opening the count, and JPMorgan today was first <https://www.jpmorganchase.com/ir/quarterly-earnings> of them all. The bank did not do amazingly – it missed earnings expectations – but things were more complicated than they seem.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
For one, it wasn’t all doom and gloom. JPMorgan’s headcount was, both compared to a year ago and compared to three months ago. Pay was up too, and the bank is on track to increase average compensation for the year by around 10% compared to 2025.
One group that will definitely benefit is JPMorgan’s M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs> bankers. The firm posted a 42% increase in M&A revenue for the first nine months of 2026 compared to 2025, ahead of Citi’s 3.4% up and Goldman’s 34% up.
Capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> teams, both equity capital markets (ECM) and debt capital markets (DCM), were not quite as successful. DCM revenue was up just 5% in the same period, compared to Citi’s 17% up and Goldman’s 29% up.
ECM revenue was up by 42% in the first nine months of the year on the same period in 2025. That was well behind Goldman, which was up 73%, and Citi, which was up 86% in the same period. This was driven by a weak performance in Q3 – JPMorgan’s ECM revenue was up by 7% compared to the same period in 2025, but that was far behind both Citi and Goldman, which were up 77% and 43%, respectively.
JPMorgan’s sales and trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> teams performed more averagely. Equities revenue, to start with, was up by 49%. That seems good. It was up more than at Citi, where equities revenue was up just 33%. It was also up less than Goldman’s 57%. JPMorgan credited its prime </news/prime-broking> and derivatives teams in particular for the performance.
Fixed income, currencies, and commodities (FICC) revenue, which was up 7.8%, was also a mixed bag. The firm was almost on par with Citi (which was 8.1% up), and well ahead of Goldman (which was 5.8% up). That 9M performance was overwhelmingly driven by a strong Q1 and Q2 – JPMorgan posted a 4.4% decrease in revenue for Q3, compared to a 3.8% increase at Citi and a milder (0.6%) decrease at Goldman.
The firm noted that revenue was lower in commodities </news/commodities-trading-hiring>, rates, credit and public finance, and only offset (positively) by currencies and emerging markets trading. The commodities failure was particularly poor; commodities have been having a bumper year due to instability in the middle east. Goldman even credited “significantly higher net revenues” in commodities as a driver behind its revenue.

item.title: Goldman Sachs & JPMorgan suggest a group of dangerous people will be paid well this year
item.description:
It's US bank results day. As predicted, things in the third quarter were not as good as in the second quarter.
The slowdown is most apparent in fixed income sales and trading. At JPMorgan, fixed income sales and trading revenues were down 4% year-on-year thanks to lower revenues in commodities, rates, credit and public finance. At Goldman Sachs, fixed income sales and trading revenues were flat year-on-year by virtue of "significantly higher" revenues in commodities and FX trading, even while revenues from mortgage, credit trading and rates trading fell.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
As bonus allocation decisions loom into view, bonuses will therefore need some careful thought. This applies equally in investment banking, where revenues are still growing, but where Goldman today said the pipeline of coming deals is less full than it was in Q2 or at the end of last year.
At both Goldman and JPMorgan, though, one group of people seem assured of comparatively generous bonuses this year: prime brokers.
As the chart below shows, equities sales and trading businesses at both banks had an exceptional third quarter, with Goldman in particular appearing to gain market share. Both banks attributed this in no small part to the effort of their prime broking teams.
Goldman, for example, said revenues were “driven by significantly higher net revenues in prime financing and portfolio financing,” and by strong revenue growth in equity derivatives intermediation. JPMorgan said revenues were driven by strong performance in prime and equity derivatives. Even at Citi, where equity derivatives sales and trading revenues inexplicably fell in Q3, prime balances were "up over 40%."
Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Citi Q3Q3 2026 revenues, $m (change on Q3 2025 in brackets)Goldman SachsJPMorganCitiAdvisoryGoldman Sachs 1,654 (+18%)JPMorgan 1,222 (+32%)Citi 406 (-4%)Equity capital marketsGoldman Sachs 666 (+43%)JPMorgan 564 (+7%)Citi 343 (+77%)Debt capital marketsGoldman Sachs 904 (+15%)JPMorgan 1,219 (+4%)Citi 601 (-3%)FICC tradingGoldman Sachs 3,471 (-1%)JPMorgan 5,366 (-4%)Citi 4,386 (+4%)Equities tradingGoldman Sachs 6,441 (+72%)JPMorgan 4,954 (+49%)Citi 1,727 (+14%)JPMorgan figures are for its Commercial & Investment Bank only. Citi advisory and underwriting figures are investment banking revenues, which include some lending and trading income. Source: company Q3 2026 earnings releases and financial supplements.
This is good news if you work in prime services, facilitating and financing trades with hedge funds and electronic trading firms, but as is increasingly being observed </news/how-to-earn-100m-at-goldman-sachs>, the growth in banks' prime broking businesses carries risks, too.
The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/d313d0ce-d552-463e-9e84-6fa8c3efeeec?syn-25a6b1a6=1>said last week that prime services revenues are expected to hit 38% of banks' equities sales and trading revenues this year and to reach nearly $48bn across the industry. Working with a single hedge fund can bring in a steady stream of $200m revenues a year (after costs) and top hedge funds are being offered 11x leverage, or twice that when derivatives are included.
If you have relationships with the top hedge funds and top trading firms, these are clearly lucrative times. However, the July losses of both Jane Street </news/jane-street-12bn-loss> and Situational Awareness </news/leopold-aschenbrenner>were reminders that lucrative times come with a risk. Neither of these losses appears to have been felt by banks' prime broking businesses, whose use of dynamic margining seems to have come a long way since the dark days of Archegos and Credit Suisse.
Nonetheless, as prime revenues grow and prime services professionals prepare for a fine bonus season, regulators are already paying attention. The FT quoted one who said: “It [prime] has just grown and grown and grown.” Questions are already being asked about whether prime businesses are too big. Giant bonuses won't help that.

item.title: Millennium poached the hot ex-Citi junior rates trader who was at Citadel
item.description:
If you work on Citi's short term interest rate trading (STIRT) desk, you can become rich like Gary Stevenson. </news/gary-stevenson-citi>You can also leave and work for a hedge fund.
Ravi Vinda spent three years on Citi's London STIRT desk before leaving for Brevan Howard. He was at Brevan Howard for four years before leaving for Citadel. He only joined Citadel in July 2025.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
We now understand that Vinda has moved again and is joining Millennium. Millennium declined to comment. Vinda didn't respond to a request to comment.
Vinda began his STIRT career in 2014 after graduating from the London School of Economics (like Stevenson). Millennium will be his third hedge fund employer since leaving Citi in 2021.
London macro headhunters complain that the talent pool has been depleted by hedge funds relentlessly posting banks' finest talent. Vinda is thought to be representative of the highly sought-after new generation. There are unconfirmed suggestions that he'll be managing a large portfolio at MLP.
Some macro funds have struggled in recent weeks </news/are-these-the-only-portfolio-managers-doing-well-during-a-brutal-month-for-macro>amidst rising rates and concerns over French government debt. It's not clear how Vinda performed during this period, but presumably Millennium was impressed.

item.title: Commodity trading’s apex predators aren’t leaving anything for their rivals
item.description:
It’s good form in the animal kingdom that after a falcon or eagle or whatever else eats its fill of a catch, it leaves the rest to go around to its less voracious neighbours. The falcons and eagles of finance, however, are somewhat less generous.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
George Carroll, head of markets recruitment in EMEA for Selby Jennings, described it in similar terms. “The hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> are where all the gaps originate from,” he said. “Hedge funds take all the best talent from all the best shops in the world.”
These days, hedge funds are hunting in commodities. </news/hedge-fund-squarepoint-is-quietly-ramping-up-its-commodities-trading-business> It’s a natural place for them to be, given instability in the Middle East and its impact on global shipping and supply chains, oil especially. The problem is that it’s somewhere that everyone wants to be </news/commodities-trading-hiring-2026>. “Everyone wants to grow in commodities at the moment,” Carroll said, “and there’s just a shortage of talent.”
The primary victims are the banks. “You have global investment banks losing their EMEA or global business heads to hedge funds,” Carroll said. Examples include Arthur Goossens, BNP’s co-head of commodities trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>, who left for Schonfeld back in February, as Bloomberg reported <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-13/schonfeld-hires-top-bnp-paribas-commodity-trader-arthur-goossens>.
It’s not just investment banks losing out, however. Commodities trading houses </news/commodities-trading-houses> are also being swept for talent by hedge funds – although they tend to have their own feeding grounds in their smaller rivals, Carroll explained.
At the highest levels, it’s also harder for hedge funds to hunt commodities traders in their own houses, on account of their exceptionally high pay – Vitol, for example, paid its partners an average of $17.6m for their work in 2024 </news/vitol-pay>. Given that hedge funds primarily attract with their generous pay, it can be hard for them to compete on that basis.
If you want to get a job at a hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, the most important thing is the ability to, and the experience of, managing risk. “That’s probably the main reason why our candidates would get rejected by a hedge fund,” Carroll said. “They haven’t got experience managing enough risk, they haven’t got experience of some sort of drawdown, they haven’t got enough experience generating significant alpha.”
As such, banks remain the best place to learn the business, even though hedge funds hire their own interns and graduates </news/hedge-funds-with-graduate-training-programmes> these days. “A lot of banks offer quite a lot of responsibility from three, four years onwards,” Carroll explained. “You can be managing a small book at four years of experience. At a hedge fund, you’re nowhere near managing anything at four years.”

item.title: A top French structurer left BNP Paribas for Nomura in Hong Kong
item.description:
French equity structurers </news/french-equity-derivative-traders-are-more-popular-then-ever-not-just-with-banks> educated in the Grandes Écoles </news/2023/02/best-grande-ecole-finance>are all the rage these days. French structurers from French banks may be even more desirable. One such structurer has emerged at Japanese bank Nomura after two and a half decades with BNP Paribas; </news/bnp-paribas-s-top-trading-professionals-are-moving-on> his new role appears to be a significant upgrade.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Maxime Lecoin has joined Nomura as a managing director and head of equity structuring for Asia (excluding Japan) and EMEA, based in the bank's Hong Kong office. He was most recently BNP Paribas' head of equity structuring for Japan, based in the bank's Tokyo office for the last three years.
Lecoin also started his career in Tokyo, but spent the bulk of his time at BNP based in its Paris headquarters. Among his many roles, he served as head of advanced pricing for equity derivatives trading, and spent seven years in sales </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> as its head of EMEA premium and digital solutions sales within equity derivatives.
Nomura's previous head of structuring in Asia was also educated at a Grande Ecole, but worked for a Swiss bank rather than a French one. Credit Suisse alum Clement Florentin </news/citadel-securities-made-another-major-equities-hire-in-hong-kong>held the role at Nomura for three years before leaving last November. He became head of structured partner solutions at Citadel Securities.
Nomura and BNP Paribas did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Citi's internal auditors are its new most important people. Hedge funds love non-compete clauses
item.description:
Working in internal audit is not the most glamorous job in financial services. It is not a front office job. It does not come with the highest compensation. For example, regulatory filings <https://www.citigroup.com/rcs/citigpa/storage/public/cgml-pillar-3-disclosures-q4-2025.pdf> show that Citi's 487 mostly senior bankers and traders in London were paid an average of $1.5m each for 2025; its seven senior control staff - of whom internal auditors are a part - received an average of only $586k.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Despite this, it's Citi's internal auditors who are suddenly abnormally important for its immediate future. As we have written here </news/citi-has-quietly-cut-7-000-jobs-this-year-what-about-the-other-9-000> often, Citi would very much like to be free of the consent orders imposed upon it by the Federal Reserve Board and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency almost exactly six years ago when it was deemed that Citi's risk management, data management and internal controls were far too weak. The bank has since invested billions and hired tens of thousands of new people </news/citi-has-quietly-cut-7-000-jobs-this-year-what-about-the-other-9-000> to make amends. It says those amends have been made. Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/citi-seeks-rapid-resolution-its-us-regulatory-burdens-2026-10-12/> says the bank's internal auditors are a hurdle to establishing this.
Reuters reports that these auditors - whose role is to monitor controls and to assure Citi's most senior people that all is functioning as it should be - have been checking the remediation work the bank's presenting to regulators so that regulatory sign off can be 'streamlined' and 'extensive checks' avoided. It's either fortunate or not, then, that Citi's internal auditors reportedly spotted an issue related to data tracing and the origin of data in its aggregated accounts earlier this summer.
It's not clear whether this issue is delaying the lifting of the consent order, which Citi has been intimating might happen soon for a while now. Even in July, Citi CEO Jane Fraser </news/citi-has-quietly-cut-7-000-jobs-this-year-what-about-the-other-9-000> suggested that the bank was "largely now operating at the Citi target state" and that at least 90% of the work had been done and validated by auditors (either internal or not).
Citi didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. The bank told Reuters that: "As we have said consistently, we will not speculate about the lifting of the consent orders because that remains solely at our regulators’ discretion," and that, "The way Citi is run today is fundamentally different from where we started our Transformation, and we are committed to ensuring the changes we have been making to strengthen our risk and control environment are sustainable."
All might become clear later today, when Citi reports its Q3 results. The lifting of the consent order is important because it's a) expensive and b) related to the ongoing employment of various people in the control functions that were expanded when the order was imposed. Citi has been cutting some of these people </news/citi-s-2026-layoffs-have-been-more-frequent-and-widespread-than-we-thought> in recent months. Internal auditors might be safe yet.
Separately, Andy Burnham in the UK wants to cut non-compete clauses which he says have "gone too far" and are holding companies back. But hedge funds like non-compete clauses and are not sure Andy is right.
The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/47b02f06-cbfc-49cb-afb8-1ae015399c4e?syn-25a6b1a6=1> notes all the hedge fund objections to doing away with non-competes. They mostly revolve around the fact that non-competes protect "commercially sensitive information" and "the proprietary investment strategies that underpin the alternative asset management industry."
We have been here before. Without non-competes, the argument goes </news/non-compete-ban-rule-banks-hedge-funds>that hedge funds would be forced to ensure that no individual knows the full secret sauce behind a trading strategy and that fund and trading firms would become havens of Taylorism with each person working on a tiny component of the process and having no view of the whole. The argument also goes that junior people and new hires would not be privy to secret information. At Citadel, for example, even some analysts </news/citadel-non-compete> are on non-competes.
As we have noted previously </news/killing-non-competes-will-make-hedge-fund-managers-more-boring-people>, though, it's about more than this. Non-competes give portfolio managers and others years off and the opportunity to travel, read poetry, and become experts at playing padel. Without them, they would be like everyone else.
Meanwhile...
Citi hired Eoghan Harrington and Christoph Heuer from BNP Paribas as managing directors within its financial sponsors team in the UK, Europe, the Middle East and Africa. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroup-hires-bnp-paribas-duo-to-bolster-financial-sponsors-in-europe-2de6c524>
Jump Trading hired Affaan Mustafa and Alejandro Soumah Fernandez, founders of Ito Markets Inc., a proprietary trading startup focused on buying and selling access to computing capacity. It also bought Ito Markets and will now have a compute trading desk. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-13/jump-trading-hires-startup-founders-to-lead-compute-desk?taid=6acdb62b50fc6400010672fa&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Two Sigma's head of talent acquisition says Two Sigma had 82 interns this summer and they completed core projects weeks before previous interns and got onto 'stretch goals.' (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/two-sigma-interns-productive-ai-skills-recruitment-2026-10>
Lone Pine's hedge fund was up 44% this year through June, but has now lost nearly all those profits after wrong-way stock bets and short wagers. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-09/lone-pine-erases-44-gain-in-brutal-quarter-on-poor-stock-bets>
“The trend is always going to be up and to the right,” said Sara Brescia O’Rear, a former pharmacist who retired in her 40s thanks to her investing success. “I’m willing to take on risk because I know it can pay off.” (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/finance/at-robinhoods-mecca-for-risk-loving-traders-everyone-has-a-tale-of-getting-rich-f960d8c2?mod=hp_lead_pos10>

item.title: An ex-hedge fund quant founded a new systematic trading firm and wants 10 'interns'
item.description:
If you are a European mathematician, particularly a European mathematician based in France, you will have heard of École polytechnique. </news/2023/02/best-grande-ecole-finance>You may also have heard of Pierre Andurand </news/2023/03/pierre-andurand-80>, the kickboxing 49-year-old trader who runs commodities </news/commodities-trading-houses> hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>Andurand Capital Management.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Adrien Chicot has both polytechnique and Andurand Capital Management on his CV </news/2023/09/investment-banking-cv-template> and has founded his own systematic trading firm, Borel Capital.
Borel Capital has an "undisclosed" amount of its own capital and is looking for 10 quantitative research </news/how-to-get-a-quant-research-job-in-a-hedge-fund> interns </jobs/quant-finance-internship?q=quant+finance+internship&countryCode=GB&radius=40&radiusUnit=km&pageSize=15&currencyCode=GBP&language=en&includeUnspecifiedSalary=true> to help invest it. "Each new joiner gets six months to build a model on any asset class. At the end of that period, if we are convinced by the model, we allocate capital to it and offer a full-time position," Chicot informs us.
The interns will be paid, but Chicot won't say how much beyond the fact that the pay will be "competitive." The first class of interns, at least will need the right to work in the EU. The next class might be more flexible.
Chicot's interns can be students. They can also be experienced investors with a few years' experience. Applicants need a degree in mathematics, physics, computer science or engineering. They will be taught how to develop a trading strategy and if capital is deployed to their strategy, they will also get paid based upon its performance.
"The real edge is that a junior gets a direct percentage of their own P&L as soon as their model goes live, rather than waiting years for it as they would at a traditional hedge fund," says Chicot.
If models don't perform, though, interns will be out. "The assessment is based on the backtest, possibly a period of paper trading, and we may hold back part of the data to keep a genuine out-of-sample window. If the model does not convince us, the internship ends there," Chicot says.
Every six months, a new cohort of interns will be hired to fill the gap. At least it's honest.

item.title: HSBC's enthusiasm for making large hires from Citi remains unblemished
item.description:
As we have written here before </news/hsbc-is-increasingly-run-by-people-who-ve-joined-from-citi>, quite a few senior people at HSBC have previously worked for Citi. It should come as no surprise, then, that the new man running the corporate and institutional banking business in EMEA and Europe, comes from Citi too.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
HSBC didn't respond to a request to comment for this article, but the bank announced last week that it has appointed Jason Rekate as head of banking for Europe and the Americas, subject to regulatory approval.
Rekate is coming from Citi, where he'd worked for 17 years and was latterly the global chair of corporate banking.
Michael Roberts, </news/hsbc-michael-roberts> who now runs HSBC's corporate and investment bank, and who also spent decades as a corporate banker at Citi, said he was "delighted" to hire Rekate. Rekate, in turn, said he was "energized" by the opportunity.
Rekate appears to be filling the hole left by the departure of Gerry Keefe </news/gerry-keefe-hsbc>. Keefe also worked with Roberts in corporate banking at Citi and was also head of banking for Europe and the Americas at HSBC.
Roberts hired Keefe (from Citi) in 2021, but to the surprise of many at HSBC, Keefe resigned in April. </news/gerry-keefe-hsbc>He now works for Golub Capital, a credit asset management firm, instead.
Keefe was based in London with HSBC. </news/hsbc-s-top-ex-citi-bankers-migrated-to-london-for-big-jobs-that-shrunk>It's not clear whether Rekate will migrate from New York.
The moves between Citi and HSBC are not all one way. Jaron Campbell, HSBC's head of corporate banking for international middle market and regions, escaped to Citi in August and is now global and north American head of network banking, a bigger job.

item.title: Barclays landed the 27-year-old whale from Nomura, but only as a VP
item.description:
If you are a big risk taker you might be named after an aquatic mammal. Barclays has landed a Nomura guy who benefits from such a moniker.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Mark 'The Whale' Wade left Nomura in June. We said that the time <https://www.linkedin.com/in/ravi-vinda-48593620/?isSelfProfile=false> that he was going to Barclays and now he has arrived. Wade wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that he was "pleased and proud" to join Barclays' London short term interest rate (STIR) desk. The FCA Register says he officially appeared there on Thursday.
Wade is a source of excitement in the London market. As we wrote in June, he is one of London's top STIR traders and has a reputation as a big risk taker. Wade is thought to have played an important role in building Nomura's sterling rates trading business.
Maybe he will do the same as Barclays where he will work with in under Hamza Hoummady, the former head of macro strats at Goldman, who runs the European rates team. Hoummady is a managing director (MD). Wade joined as a VP.
By our estimation, Wade is aged only 27, so he has ample time to become a managing director himself. Alternatively, Barclays' macro desk has a long history of launching hedge fund careers. </news/barclays-macro-to-hedge-funds>
Barclays rates desk is widely expected to promote star rates salesman Puni Raja </news/barclays-macro-to-hedge-funds> to MD in December. Raja, who runs UK real money sales, is thought to have made huge profits for the bank this year. Alongside Kristen Macleod, Barclays' global head of macro distribution, Raja is understood to have made the closing remarks at Barclays' macro conference in Paris last week.

item.title: JPMorgan brought in a new MD in New York, from Deutsche Bank in London
item.description:
It’s not always easy to come back to your career after a few years out. Sometimes, however, you end up as a managing director </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> (MD) at JPMorgan in New York, and all is well.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Matthew Friend will join JPMorgan in New York later this month as a MD in the firm’s technology leveraged finance team. Friend left his last employer, seemingly Deutsche Bank, some years ago when his team was being pushed hard </news/deutsche-bank-s-london-tmt-juniors-keep-leaving-allegedly-due-to-overwork> by its bosses. He spent 13 years in total at Deutsche, working first San Francisco and then London.
Friend did not respond to a request for comment, but after leaving Deutsche Bank, we reported that </news/deutsche-bank-s-london-tmt-juniors-keep-leaving-allegedly-due-to-overwork> he was looking for a new role in San Francisco. It appears he did not find it.
Tech leveraged finance is a very interesting seat to be in. On one hand, some half a trillion dollars will be spent last year in AI-related debt, Morgan Stanley estimated <https://www.reuters.com/business/global-ai-debt-issuance-top-500-billion-2026-morgan-stanley-says-2026-06-10/>. On the other, that same boom has caused a massive wave of downgrades for traditional software firms, many of whom now are dealing with higher borrowing costs and tougher scrutiny. Software firms in turn were <https://finance.yahoo.com/news/software-companies-face-higher-borrowing-110348553.html> postponing fundraising efforts. Technology giveth, and technology taketh away.

item.title: HSBC's bigger bonuses: senior bankers got £620k last year, others got £12k
item.description:
HSBC would like people to know that it's getting stricter about compensation.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-12/hsbc-moves-to-wall-street-bonus-model-as-it-cuts-fixed-pay-deals?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261012&utm_campaign=author_20887312>reported today that HSBC will - in future - be paying a higher proportion of pay as bonuses and a lower proportion of pay in salaries and that it will be phasing out its role-related allowances. </news/2023/02/allowances-bankers-london>
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
An HSBC spokesman informed us: “As a global bank, adapting our approach in this way strengthens our ability to pay for performance, better differentiate, attract the best talent, and recognise those who deliver the best outcomes for our customers, clients and stakeholders.”
This should come as a shock to no one. HSBC already declared earlier this year that it would be paying its bonuses on an "eat what you kill basis" </news/hsbc-bonus-worries>and senior people classified as material risk takers (MRTs) in HSBC's investment bank have already had their pay skewed towards bonuses as follows:
Salaries (fixed pay), including allowances, fell 7.5% to $584k (£441k) for MRTs in the investment bank between 2023 and 2025 according to HSBC's regulatory filings. Bonuses rose 6% over the same period to $819k (£620k).
Bonuses could rise a lot more. Liberated from the bonus cap, HSBC has reserved the right to pay bonuses that are 10x salaries </news/bonus-cap>if it wants. However, there is little sign so far that a lot more senior people have received huge bonuses. Regulatory filings show that last year, the number of material risk takers earning over €5m (£4.2m) at HSBC fell to its lowest level since 2022.
While HSBC is cutting salaries and promising bonuses aligned to performance for its top people, most employees at the bank seem to be having the opposite experience. Last year, the median amount of combined bonus, pension and non-salary benefits at HSBC in the UK was a mere £11.7k, which was down from £17.5k in 2023. The median salary at HSBC in the UK rose from £46k to £58k over the same period. Many of HSBC's UK staff don't work in the investment bank, though.
As HSBC focuses on pay for performance in the investment bank, it is cutting various perks </news/hsbc-perks-hong-kong>alongside the popular role related allowances which have the advantage of being paid no matter how well you do. It is doing so gently, though. HSBC's senior bankers will only get their allowances cut from 2028. HSBC's senior bankers in Hong Kong with six children will still get school fees paid if they work for the bank already - only new joiners will have to pay the school fees themselves.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Ex-Barclays traders want to sue Barclays. Why now is a fine time to start your life in private equity
item.description:
As we predicted here </news/christian-bittar-deutsche-bank> last week, Christian Bittar, the legendary Deutsche Bank rates trader who once made a bonus of $140m </news/christian-bittar> while speaking softly and eating boiled eggs and junk food, and who was imprisoned for nearly two years, has had his conviction for conspiracy to defraud via manipulation of the Euribor rate quashed. So, too, have five former traders from Barclays.
Now they want vengeance. And that could be expensive.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The latest quashing of the convictions came after Tom Hayes </news/tom-hayes-carlo-palombo-supreme-court>, an ex-UBS trader, and Carlo Palombo, another ex-Barclays trader, had their own convictions for manipulating benchmark lending rates quashed last year. The British Supreme Court <https://supremecourt.uk/uploads/uksc_2024_0087_0088_judgment_f9b6ff1bb1.pdf>deemed that the jury had been wrongly instructed by a judge, who'd said that if Hayes took the commercial interests of the bank into account when influencing Libor rates, the rate he suggested was necessarily improper. The subsequent convictions of Bittar (who pleaded guilty because, the FT <https://www.ft.com/content/d16e8abb-ce63-4ed4-b2f2-3a0805e9cab1?syn-25a6b1a6=1> says, the court rulings at the time meant that he felt that he had no viable defence) and the other five Barclays traders hinged on this judge's wrongful advice. Once Hayes' conviction had been overturned, the rest seemed bound to follow.
Hayes himself is already suing UBS for $400m </news/tom-hayes-ubs-400m> for 'malicious prosecution' after he says the Swiss bank unfairly framed him as the "evil mastermind" of Libor rigging simply because he was a bit vulnerable and the "perfect fall guy." Speaking to the Sunday Times <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/barclays-libor-traders-speak-out-qj7wjh55k>at the weekend, two of the exonerated Barclays traders - Alex Pabon and Jay Merchant - said they would consider suing Barclays too.
Pabon told The Times he'd been made a "scapegoat" and that his life had been consumed by the overturned conviction. "When these investigations started, I was 31 years old. That was when I was first contacted about the Libor investigation. And I’m 48 years old now; 31 to 48 — it’s your prime working age, and for me it’s really been consumed by Libor.”
There is one single trader conviction yet to be overturned. It concerns Peter Johnson, another former Barclays trader, who was sacked after 30 years with the bank in 2012 and then jailed for two years for manipulating interest rates. Speaking to the BBC <https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-65916892>three years ago, Johnson said the conviction took a huge toll on his mental health. "[When I woke up] I'd have about five seconds when I thought all was well with the world. And then I'd realise that it wasn't. And I'd go around all day with a sort of a weight pressing against my chest. I'd wait for six o'clock before I started self-medicating with alcohol. I had panic attacks."
Johnson too now wants his conviction overturned. When he does, he too may want to sue Barclays. Ironically, before his conviction Johnson had even raised concerns about Barclays ‘low-balling’ its Libor submissions and wanted to set them higher, but leaked audio recordings obtained by the BBC showed him being pressured to keep them low. "In my most optimistic view, I would like my guilty plea to be revoked. I'd like to basically have my reputation restored. And I'd like senior people to be held accountable," said Johnson back in 2023.
Not all the exonerated Barclays traders are coming after the bank. Colin Bermingham told the Times that life is too short: “I’m 70 years old … This is going to be a long, drawn-out process. I’ve already invested too much of my life in having this all hanging over me.” Barclays may only hope that others feel similarly.
Separately, much has been said about the fact that leaving banking for private equity </news/leaving-banking-private-equity> doesn't seem like a good move nowadays, but maybe that's wrong?
Private equity bosses think so. Gathered together at a summit held by the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/b42bb760-3eda-430d-adfd-69c359425c1d?syn-25a6b1a6=1> in London, they said now's a fine time to start a career in PE. Dipan Patel, co-chief executive of UK-headquartered buyout group Permira, declared, for example, that the current vintage of PE deals "will be among the better" and that the "top quartile will have exceptional returns."
This is because high rates aren't a problem once everyone accepts the new world. “It’s a problem to be in a low-rate environment,” explained Patel. “Being in a high-rate environment, eyes wide open, is not a problem for private equity because it translates into deal pricing.”
Julian Salisbury, who was once the highest earning person </news/2023/09/goldman-sachs-julian-salisbury> at Goldman Sachs, was also at the Summit. He said that even the "pig in the python" companies stuck in buyout portfolios have the potential to make money for funds. These pigs need debt or equity investors to "provide them incremental financing so that they can refinance and extend the hold of the asset.”
Meanwhile...
The third quarter for banks wasn't as good as previous quarters and this may make it hard to allocate bonuses. “For the first half of the year it’s almost like everybody won, and now that might not be the case,” Mike Mayo said. “There’s likely a wider dispersion this quarter between the winners and losers.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-09/goldman-sachs-gs-poised-to-lead-wall-street-s-19-billion-stock-trading-haul>
Data centre company Firmus Grid pulled its $30bn IPO, thereby delaying the redemption of its co-founder, who once served time in prison on insider trading charges. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-09/ex-banker-s-redemption-story-hits-a-setback-as-firmus-pulls-ipo>
Who will be the future COO of Goldman Sachs. Could it be Denis Coleman? Could it be Ashok Varadhan? (Reuters <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/waldrons-expected-rise-stirs-talk-inside-goldman-knock-on-succession-plans-2026-10-09/>)
100,000 people applied for Revolut's internships and graduate programmes. That's 330 per job. (The Banker) <https://www.thebanker.com/content/07c93749-93bc-4dbf-b680-6fd67c45bb8b>
What it's like when you get an internship at Susquehanna: “When I got the offer call and they said how much the salary was, I asked a few times if they were saying the right number. I can’t fathom how an intern should be making that much money.” (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/the-race-is-already-on-for-next-summers-50-000-internships-3db6f96e?mod=WSJ_home_feature_6_pos_1>
Jennifer Davey, early careers recruitment manager at Deutsche Bank said you can stand out during applications by elaborating on why a transaction interested you as well as the strategic rationale behind it and why you think it reflects Deutsche Bank’s broader capabilities. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/e540f9e7-04c4-47c1-ba07-2fdf8dd9a31c?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
How to leave your career as a professional tennis player and get a job at Goldman Sachs. “I took 342 meetings to get to know different people in 2025. I met over 15 different people at Goldman. I joined through a kind of internship programme. I did eight formal interviews within the span of three days..." (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/sport/tennis/article/milos-raonic-andy-murray-goldman-sachs-2wqdm8xgl>
EY cut jobs in America last year but it hired for its global service centres and centralized tech functions and so increased headcount 12%. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/05f80d05-c80f-48ff-a65d-f379d77ed8af?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Ryan, a US tax firm, wants to hire and promote 100 partners in the UK and Europe in the next three years. (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/big-four-challenger-ryan-goes-on-a-hiring-spree-in-uk-and-europe-8l3bpm39z>
There is a new trend for "loud working" in which people try to ensure their work is visible and gets noticed. (Business Insider) <https://www.businessinsider.com/loud-working-job-security-layoffs-linkedin-promotions-2026-10?utm_source=Iterable&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=News%20Alert%20Bucket%201A%20-%20loud-working-job-security-layoffs-linkedin-promotions-2026-10&insiderId=d8198f66-3051-484f-bdc4-3c5b70be622d>
The nice thing about bonds is that if you're right, you get paid no matter what anyone else thinks. Bill Gross would look at high-yield bonds that were about to mature, but still carried high interest rates that implied ridiculous odds of the company running into financial trouble in the next few months. (The Diff) <https://www.thediff.co/archive/longreads-open-thread-204/?ref=the-diff-newsletter>
How trend following funds make money: you lose small and often but then make money once a trend becomes established. (Navnoor Bawar) <https://www.navnoorbawaresearch.com/p/how-man-ahls-trend-following-makes?utm_source=substack&publication_id=5040435&post_id=219046919&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>
Greg Coffey's </news/2012/10/greg-coffey-is-hedge-fund-management-is-incompatible-with-fatherhood-ageing> Kirkoswald Asset Management had a good September and has returned 20% this year. (With Intelligence) <https://platform.withintelligence.com/login?redirect=%2Finsights%2Fkirkoswald-posts-4-sept-gains-up-more-than-20-ytd%3Fp%3D126644%26a%3D1099324>
"We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose." (Anthropic) <https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email>

item.title: The Coffee Run: What's the point of quitting banking for private equity?
item.description:
We've launched a new weekly video series <https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLqJc_c5JT66B3Cp_26xsN8Xsv2EtvtEQQ> to accompany Morning Coffee, in which we look at one story in more depth to give you the full picture.
To PE or not to PE? That is the question.
Generations of bankers have faced this choice and, in the past, it seemed a lot more cut and dry than it is today. Years of decline in the private equity sector, combined with various initiatives from banks to retain their staff make moving to the buy side harder than ever.
For many, it's still worth it. Find out why on The Coffee Run.

item.title: The Wilderness Diaries, Episode 1: Access Denied
item.description:
I had just returned from a short compassionate leave when my regular fortnightly catch-up turned into something else entirely. An HR officer slipped quietly into the room. Within seconds, I understood: I was being made redundant </news/2019/07/what-happens-after-you-lose-your-banking-job>from my job with a major bank in London.
I was stunned. I had not seen it coming.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Discretion, I was told, was key. I would wait in the HR officer's office rather than return to my desk, so as not to alarm colleagues. When I was finally allowed back, my phone was dead, my laptop locked, my access card useless.
Twenty years in finance, switched off in the time it takes to drink a coffee. I was 53, one of a wave of people let go by a reputable financial firm. It had nothing to do with performance; my reviews were consistently excellent. It came down to a headcount number on a spreadsheet.
What follows is something nobody prepares you for. The French call it la traversée du désert, the crossing of the desert. Here, the desert is the job marke </news/london-banking-jobs-fallen>t. The headlines said London's unemployment was low, so I was confident I would bounce back fast. Not out of revenge, but because I wanted to show my former employer they had made a mistake.
Six months and more than 200 CVs </news/2023/09/investment-banking-cv-template> later, I have very few interviews </news/banking-interviews> and a collection of stories: friends who went quiet, recruiters who ghosted me, </news/poor-treatment-banking-recruiters>algorithms that never gave me a chance, and a Jobcentre Plus experience that deserves a column of its own. There is the company where I sent ten referred applications and never received a single screening call. There are the ex-colleagues who ask, kindly, whether the job market is tough. Over it all sits a constant weight, mental and physical, that I did not expect
I thought I was alone. Not lonely, exactly. But alone. I could barely look at the people streaming into the offices around Canary Wharf, Bank and Liverpool Street. It wasn't jealousy. That came later. It was the feeling that I had become useless, a weight on society, a laughing stock. Then a friend, made redundant at the same time as me, sent me an article <https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/morgan-stanley-jobs-wall-street-banking-tech-ai-b2932534.html >, and the penny dropped. The job cuts in UK banking have been brutal in the past few years and as AI is rolled out there are even more cuts to come. </news/hsbc-wealth-cuts>
I now know that I am not alone at all. I was simply wrong. Getting a new job will not be easy, not at all.

item.title: NatWest Markets' trading MDs are fretting after yesterday's unexpected cuts
item.description:
As we reported yesterday </news/natwest-close-government-bond-trading>, NatWest Markets is closing its US and European government bond desks and withdrawing from primary dealership programmes outside the UK. Insiders fear that this is only the start.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
NatWest didn't comment for this article, but a spokesperson yesterday said the cuts will allow the bank to focus resources on other areas. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-08/natwest-pulls-back-from-dealing-us-and-european-government-bonds>said these areas will include the financing business and insiders say that Stuart Connell, head of private financing at NatWest Markets will now have a bigger role within the markets business.
The changes do not appear to have been anticipated. Multiple sources say they came as a surprise yesterday, even to managing directors. Many are now fretting that there will be more cuts to come - even though only around 10 jobs have been put at risk so far, there are fears that this will grow in time.
Material risk takers, including senior traders, at NatWest earned an average of $1m last year according to NatWest's Pillar 3 filing for 2025. <https://investors.natwestgroup.com/~/media/Files/R/RBS-IR-V2/results-center/13022026/nwm-pillar-3-report.pdf>There are suggestions that top traders at the bank are paid generously given individual PnL that is diminutive compared to rival banks. There are also unconfirmed suggestions that some of those leaving generated higher PnL than some of those staying.
Although NatWest is closing its European and U.S. primary dealership programmes, it remains committed to the UK gilt market and to support clients in the UK and Europe. From Q1 2027, it will be focused on fixed income and markets financing, currencies and debt capital markets.

item.title: Goldman Sachs tripled French headcount and is still going for "ambitious growth" in Paris
item.description:
It hasn't been a great few months for French M&A activity. Data provider Dealogic says M&A revenues in France fell 46% year-on-year in the third quarter, driving a 29% decline in all investment banking revenues in the country.
Despite this, Céline Méchain, co-head of investment banking in the French speaking region, says on LinkedIn that Goldman is "pursuing an ambitious growth strategy" in France, and is hiring.
Goldman has already tripled Paris headcount in the past five years, says Méchain. Its ambitious growth strategy has also involved the addition of David Benichou from Morgan Stanley in July, to be Méchain's co-head. Benichou said he was excited about this.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Dealogic says Goldman ranked only 10th for M&A in France in the first nine months of this year, behind even Houlihan Lokey. During the same period last year, it ranked 5th. Benichou was head of investment banking for France at Morgan Stanley and might be expected to improve matters. Morgan Stanley, however, ranked outside the top 10 for French M&A during the first nine months of 2026.
Méchain says Goldman's French growth plans involve major corporations and entrepreneurial and family-owned businesses. The firm is hiring "classic associates" in Paris to help support this.
Although Méchain says Goldman's French headcount has tripled since 2021, it's not clear how much of this growth occurred recently. Goldman Sachs' CEO David Solomon </news/david-solomon-goldman-sachs> said <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-05-13/goldman-s-solomon-sees-france-making-more-pro-business-strides>in mid-2024 that the firm had tripled Paris headcount in the five previous years. Two year ago, the firm moved Dirk Lievens <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-04-22/goldman-to-add-dealmakers-in-paris-as-financial-m-a-heats-up> from London to Paris to run financial institutions group (FIG) M&A for Europe from the French capital, but Benichou excepted much of this year's hiring there seems to have been very junior.
Goldman Sachs declined to comment.

item.title: Morning Coffee: How to earn a $100m bonus at Goldman Sachs. Why prime broking businesses are so special
item.description:
It is possible to earn $100m at Goldman Sachs. It may take more than one year to do so. Ed Emerson </news/2023/12/ed-emerson-goldman-sachs>, the former Goldman star commodities trader who retired aged 47 in 2023, was said to have been paid $100m over the three years previously. Now, Goldman CEO David Solomon </news/david-solomon-goldman-sachs> will be earning $100m too, for his cumulative efforts since 2021.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Solomon's $100m was valued at only $17m when he was awarded it, but it has swelled in value after meeting performance conditions relating to Goldman's absolute share price, Goldman's dividends, and Goldman's share price relative to peers like Bank of America, Citigroup, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and Wells Fargo. Many of these performance conditions have been far exceeded and so Solomon will receive $100m - maybe more - once the award cliff vests at the end of October. All he will then need to do is to wait another year and the money will be his.
The new windfall might be why Solomon is thinking of retiring as CEO in 2028. It's also not his only $100m. He's also been paid around $250m in "regular" salaries and bonuses since 2018, plus another $80m retention award with a five year cliff vest for 2030, which will still pay out if he hangs around at Goldman in some capacity. This retention award would be worth around $116m at Goldman's current share price.
All of this suggests that earning $100m at Goldman is partly a question of patience. Solomon isn't alone in getting a payment at the end of October. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-08/goldman-sachs-ceo-david-solomon-top-executives-to-earn-massive-bonus-payouts>notes that 19 members of Goldman's management committee in 2021 are getting a share of a similar payout, now worth $400m. This was awarded around the same time as Solomon's to keep them all happy in 2021 and is subject to the same performance and retention conditions. These people include John Waldron, </news/john-waldron-goldman-sachs-ceo> Ashok Varadhan </news/2018/05/ashok-varadhan-goldman-sachs>, Dan Dees </news/dan-dees-goldman-sachs> and Marc Nachmann </news/2023/11/goldman-asset-management>. Waldron and Dees probably need the money: between them, they have 11 children.
Maybe they deserve it. Goldman's share price has soared since March 2024, rising from $386 to a peak of $1,062 in June. However, the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/9db7a522-17a2-40c9-a0e5-ee250992be06?syn-25a6b1a6=1> observed last year that Goldman has been a particular beneficiary of deregulation under the Trump presidency, and had seized upon this to slash its core tier one equity capital ratio from 15.1% to 13.3% and increase its total assets by 8%. This suggests that friendly regulation helps if you want to earn $100m. Goldman's shares have done particularly well under Trump II. It also helps that David Solomon was finally persuaded to exit the loss-making consumer business he'd previously championed.
All that Goldman's executives need to hope now is that the share price doesn't fall too much further before the 2021 awards vest at the end of October.
Separately, it's a great time to work in prime broking </news/prime-broking-banks-2026>. With memories of Archegos Capital Management in the deep past, the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/d313d0ce-d552-463e-9e84-6fa8c3efeeec?syn-25a6b1a6=1>reports that the revenues banks make by lending to hedge funds have gone through the roof.
Coalition Greenwich reportedly expects prime revenues to hit 38% of equities sales and trading revenues this year (up from 10% two decades ago) and total prime broking revenues to hit $47.9bn. The FT says a single hedge fund can generate a revenue stream of $200m a year after trading costs (Goldman reportedly <https://www.ft.com/content/bdec4129-ccac-4149-aa53-90ddd50cb925?syn-25a6b1a6=1>generated $200m in fees from Situational Awareness, for example).
What could go wrong? Credit Suisse famously lost $5.5bn </news/2021/11/credit-suisse-prime-broking-shutdown> through the "incompetence" of its prime brokers in dealing with Archegos. The FT says the Bank of England has its eye on things. The Federal Reserve says prime brokers are now offering 11x leverage to the biggest hedge funds, and this doesn't include derivative exposures, which can increase leverage to 25 times for hedge funds and 40 times for electronic trading firms. Sounds great for prime brokers, while it lasts.
Meanwhile...
Kevin Sneader, Goldman's president of Asia Pacific ex-Japan, says: “When our young folks now start work, they’re managing agents...They have to make the most of this virtual army that they’ve now got.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-08/young-bankers-to-manage-ai-agents-from-start-goldman-exec-says?cmpid=banking-industry&utm_campaign=banking-industry&utm_medium=email&utm_source=newsletter&utm_term=261008&utm_content=9841>
Andy Burnham wants to do away with non-compete clauses in the UK. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/297ca864-737c-4112-b368-f21a20cc78d2?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Citi hired Rogier Pop, who was JPMorgan's head of EMEA capital goods. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroup-hires-jpmorgan-dealmaker-pop-to-lead-diversified-industrials-in-europe-d09218bd>
Deutsche Bank hired David Garland from BP to help it expand US power trading. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-06/deutsche-bank-hires-bp-trader-garland-for-rebuild-in-us-power?taid=6ac62641a01597000145bb0f&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Alex Evangeli from Virtu joined Goldman Sachs for fixed income ETF trading. (Fi Desk) <https://www.fi-desk.com/evangeli-swaps-virtu-for-goldman/>
156,000 students entered the World Quant international quant championship this year, almost double last year's total. 75,000 were solo entries working with AI. (FT) < https://www.ft.com/content/ec8b74b6-0cf7-4ded-abd4-85bde8a80df4?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Banks are cutting tech headcount in India. Citigroup has hired a net 2,000 people in India so far this year, down from about 4,000 last year. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-10-07/ai-crowds-out-fresh-grads-at-wall-street-tech-hubs-in-india?taid=6ac6efca8ff35e0001f90242&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
How to impress partners at Goldman Sachs. “Did you fail any levels of the CFA?” Brevity is confidence, I thought, and answered simply: “Nope.” (NoRebates) <https://norebates.substack.com/p/miracles>

item.title: When bankers earning $700k blow their money and lose their jobs
item.description:
Matt Connolly </news/ivy-league-wall-street>has experienced the good side of working on a trading floor in an investment bank. And he has experienced the very bad side.
Connolly spent nearly two decades as a trader on Wall Street, rising to become a senior trader on Deutsche Bank's derivatives trading desk in New York. Connolly says he made good money, but it ended badly.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In 2016, Connolly lost his job at Deutsche Bank and was accused of manipulating the LIBOR rate. In 2019, he was convicted and sentenced to home confinement. Four years later, though, he was acquitted. Connolly sued Deutsche Bank for $150m, which settled out of court in 2024. He's written a book <https://www.amazon.com/dp/0999757237> about his experiences and is a man of leisure with an active account on X. <https://x.com/MConnollyittm>
Writing there <https://x.com/MConnollyittm/status/2104303195933622721?s=20>a few weeks ago, Connolly said there was a time in 2005 when he paid a guy $400k for two years in a row (nearly $700k at today's prices) and gave him two years' notice that his job was disappearing. However, when the trader's job did, subsequently, disappear, Connolly said the trader complained that he was "broke/desperate." - "His Porsche was a year old. Dude WTF are you thinking?," Connolly added.
Elaborating on this post, Connolly says there's always a portion of people in banking who overspend. "Just like professional sports, a certain portion of bankers take one good year of pay, project that out 30 years, and start spending that way. Not realizing it rarely works that way."
With mortgage costs rising, high end London house prices falling and banking jobs at risk of automation, Connolly's cautionary tale has new relevance. There's limited sympathy for people who work in financial services, he tells us, but most are just normal people. Most don't earn $700k and don't buy new Porsches but are nonetheless subject to the vagaries of the brutal employment cycle. "Accountants, back office people, IT staff, just regular people making a living." No one, though, should spend as if their jobs are secure. Financial services is a notoriously erratic industry.
