item.title: The early years of Blackstone's Steve Schwarzman: A "bleak and depressing" banking job and a "dull" MBA
item.description:
What does it take to become CEO of one of the largest private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> firms in the world? There's no better person to ask than Stephen Schwarzman, founder of Blackstone </news/do-you-still-need-an-investment-banking-graduate-job-to-get-hired-by-blackstone>. His story is well known, but a new series of articles <https://www.blackstone.com/my-personal-history/>released by Blackstone in partnership with Nikkei Asia have provided new insights on his rise to the top.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
He grew up in "a rough neighbourhood."
Schwarzman grew up in Oxford Circle, "then a Jewish neighborhood in Philadelphia." His family ran a curtain and linen store there for several generations; Schwarzman said his father ran the store with a "perfectionism not unlike the discipline" he had when building Blackstone. His father worked seven days per week.
Schwarzman said "Oxford Circle in those days was a rough place," and that the father of his friend was killed by the mafia. His family later moved to an upper-middle-class suburb which he described as "a different America." The Schwarzman family home was "only slightly better than an ordinary house, with a lawn and two family cars."
He was failing his degree at Yale, then got some help
Schwarzman took an "unusual interdisciplinary program" at Yale University called "Human Culture and Behavior." His first papers were on English literature; he struggled on the first one and then "unquestionably fail[ed]" the second. An English teacher then took him aside and tutored him; "he taught me first how to write and then how to analyze."
"His kindness changed the course of my life," Schwarzman said. Not only did his grades improve to the point where he was in the top 10% of the class, Schwarzman said he gained the "confidence" to try and break into Yale's illustrious Skull and Bones club. He was invited to join after he was able to organize for the New York City Ballet to perform on campus, which he did by pretending to represent the Yale Ballet Society (which did not exist).
He haggled his graduate salary with the founder of an investment bank
Like many people in private equity </news/junior-bankers-still-want-to-work-in-private-equity-i-hate-my-life-now-it-s-just-a-question-of-getting-in>, Schwarzman started his career as an investment banker </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>, spending seven months at midsize bank DLJ which was his "doorway to Wall Street."
Schwarzman is infamous for turning down DLJ's initial offer of $10k (roughly $90k today) because he wanted to be the highest earning graduate of his class. He had heard that another student was offered $10k too and asked Bill Donaldson, one DLJ's founders, if he could be paid $10.5k instead. Schwarzman said Donaldson was "astonished" but said he would think about it. The next day, Schwarzman got his wish.
"My good fortune ended there," Schwarzman said. "No one bothered to teach me anything. It was one of the most frightening experiences I had ever had." He described the seven months at DLJ as "bleak and depressing," and left to pursue a Harvard MBA, but he did enough to impress Donaldson; Schwarzman said that he received an offer to lead DLJ as the firms president when he was 34, which he turned down.
He found his Harvard MBA "dull."
Schwarzman went back to school to get an MBA </news/best-mba-for-finance-banking> at Harvard because he "had struggled badly for lack of any real knowledge of finance" while working in banking.
Harvard was disappointing, though. Schwarzman said the school had "no brilliant students" He grew restless "listening to such tedious lessons in the company of students who did not seem especially clever," but was persuaded to stay after writing to Dick Jenrette, one of DLJ's founders.
After graduating from Harvard Business School, Schwarzman received an offer to work at Lehman Brothers </news/investment-bank-associates-today-earn-less-than-the-weakest-2007-lehman-brothers-associates>. There, he met Pete Peterson, with whom he founded Blackstone. "Connections with people can change a life," Schwarzman said, "provided you are open enough to ask them anything."

item.title: Millennium just rehired Balyasny's top macro PM in London
item.description:
Where is James Watson? Not, it seems at Balyasny Asset Management (BAM) in London. Not any more.
Bloomberg reported Watson's exit from BAM an hour ago. We understand that he is returning to Millennium.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Millennium and BAM declined to comment for this article. Watson didn't respond to a request to comment.
Watson joined BAM from Millennium in London in September 2024. He spent nearly seven years at Millennium and is thought to have run a pod of over 20 people there.
Watson built a pod at Balyasny too, although it was smaller. It is not clear what will become of this, although various people appear to have left already. The exits are understood to include Aditya Singh and George Tyrrell who joined from Goldman Sachs in 2024 and who both left in July according to the FCA Register. Olek Gajowniczek </news/another-nomura-rates-md-leaves-this-time-for-hedge-fund-balyasny>from Nomura is also thought to be/have been in Watson's pod. There are suggestions that John Sun at BAM in New York is going to Millennium too.
If Watson is indeed returning to Millennium, his brief sojourn at Balyasny looks expensive for the smaller fund. Headhunters say Watson was an expensive hire; so too were members of his team.

item.title: Cambridge University student with 8 bank spring weeks dispenses advice
item.description:
It’s the tail-end of application season if you want to do a spring week </news/banking-spring-week-advice> at an investment bank. If you don’t know what those are, it’s a bit late to find out, but they’re basically week-long insight days hosted by banks for first-year students, usually in London, that also often come with a summer internship </news/internship-investment-bank> offer.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Students can apply to as many spring internships as they want, and can do more than one if the timings match. A few years ago, LSE student God’sFavour Oluwanusin </news/spring-week-internship-banking> had nine spring internships. A few years before that, another LSE student named Haydn had eleven </news/2014/12/meet-economics-student-completed-11-finance-internships-first-year>. Haydn is now a director in Barclays' debt capital markets (DCM) team.
This year, in a perhaps more competitive application environment, Cambridge student Daniyaal Anawar got eight spring internships. In a blog post <https://daniyaalanawar.com/guides/how-i-got-8-spring-week-offers/> detailing what worked for him, prefacing that he can’t prove that any of it did work, he offers some interesting insights for prospective spring interns.
Anawar first bit of advice is not to live and die by the obvious choices. “There’s more to life than just IBD,” Anawar says, and that the best thing to do would be to research and pick “what you are most interested in.”
Some of the advice is well-known. Work experience in finance helps, especially with big firms. If you're a UK student, you should have an AAB at A-Level at a minimum (“If you have lower grades, look into corporate banking,” Anawar said); and you should note the specific results of your experiences, rather than just give generic descriptions.
Anawar also has some more niche tips. For example, he says you should always wear a suit and tie when doing a pre-recorded HireVue </news/hirevue-questions-banking> interview. He says you should smile, be “giddy” and likeable.
In fact, a big focus of Anawar’s advice concerns likeability. In a live interview, “you don't want them walking away just neutral on you,” and that means reading your interviewer. “Adjust if they seem engaged or if they've checked out,” he said. Even during an assessment centre, dealing with people who “say dumb stuff sometimes” means disagreeing “without being annoying about it.”
And, of course, being likeable is a project that stretches into your very hobbies. Don’t just say you’re a football fan, say that you’re a “loyal Arsenal” fan (other teams presumably are okay to note here). “Boxing, go-karting, content creation” is “way more interesting.” Anawar says.
Of course, if you don’t get a spring week, it’s not the end of the world. You can still get a second year summer internship the normal way, but expect it to be an uphill battle: Trackr noted </news/spring-internships-uk> last year that a sizeable chunk of spring weeks were not convertible into a summer internship. This year, even less are </news/spring-internships-2026>.

item.title: These are awkward times for the Citi investment banking analysts who weren't promoted
item.description:
Investment banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank>analysts </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> at Citi are talented people and private equity </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> firms would like to hire them.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This is the informed opinion of David Friedland, Citi’s ex-Goldman new co-head of North America investment banking. Friedland told Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-07/private-equity-isn-t-slowing-its-poaching-of-bankers-citi-executive-says> yesterday that Citi has “top talent and top talent has opportunities.”
It is reportedly </news/now-citi-will-promote-even-its-moderately-good-analysts-to-associate-after-two-years> to stop this top talent from pursuing private equity opportunities that Citi will begin promoting all its analysts to associates in two years rather than three next summer. Early promotions mean higher salaries </news/citi-salaries-london> and higher bonuses.
However, early promotions may also be problematic because not all Citi analysts are talented equally.
As we noted this week, Citi was already offering its analysts an expedited associate track. It was just not offering the fast track to everyone. Juniors at the bank in London tell us that only around 70% of second year analysts were told by their managing directors (MDs) that they’d be converted to associates early last summer.
That 70% are now associates 0. They will become full associates in January 2027, around two and a half years after joining Citi. When they do, sources say their salaries in London will go from £85k to £110k. They have already received an extra £20k bonus for making associate.
That’s good news for the 70%. However, it’s less good news for the circa 30% of Citi second year analysts who didn’t get the early promotion to associate a few months ago because their MDs thought they weren’t ready. They must wait.
The circa 30% won’t make associate 0 until July 2027, by which time they will have been Citi analysts for a full three years. However, in July 2027 Citi is also planning to promote its entire class of 2nd year analysts to associate 0s under the new expedited scheme it announced this week.
Citi insiders say this state of affairs is already causing some grumbling. Analysts who’ve done a full three years and whose promotions were delayed by MDs will be sitting alongside analysts who’ve only worked two years and who were promoted irrespective of performance. “It’s very frustrating for them,” says one insider.
Fortunately, Citi will only have this problem once. On balance, Citi juniors say that shortening the analyst cycle was the right thing to do – most other banks have done it already and this just brings Citi in line with everywhere else.
Citi didn’t respond to a request to comment.

item.title: NatWest's trader job cuts send shiver through the market
item.description:
NatWest is closing its US and European government bond desks and withdrawing from primary dealership programmes outside the UK. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-08/natwest-pulls-back-from-dealing-us-and-european-government-bonds> reported the move earlier today and said up to 10 jobs are at risk.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
A spokesperson for NatWest told us the bank is "simplifying" its structure and focusing its resources on areas of strongest customer growth and demand. These areas are deemed to be UK primary dealership, plus fixed income and markets financing, currencies and debt capital markets (DCM).
People on the desks being exited are still officially employed by NatWest. It's not clear who is at risk, but NatWest's euro government traders include the likes of Marc Moulin and Axel Didio in Paris, and Ryan Hearity and Adam Denning in London. Salespeople are thought to have been affected too.
NatWest's reason for closing the desks right now isn't clear. It has been a difficult few weeks in macro trading. Rokos made money <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-07/hedge-fund-rokos-returned-4-2-in-turbulent-month-for-trading> in September, but many hedge funds did not. </news/are-these-the-only-portfolio-managers-doing-well-during-a-brutal-month-for-macro>It's not clear whether banks have lost money too. NatWest may be the first bank to respond to the challenges.
Equally, though, traders at rival banks point to longer term harsh effects of electronification. European government bonds are traded through platforms like MTS Euronext and as volatility has risen, traders say costs can be prohibitively high for the more marginal players. "This could bode badly for the likes of HSBC, Santander, or even UBS," suggests one.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Deutsche Bank’s most legendary trader has a big day coming. Hedge fund manager loses billions but gets another $1.5bn back
item.description:
“Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it’s about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened”. Jonathan Mathew <https://www.ft.com/content/9c61d1a4-c982-41d5-a96e-f06df406c7e9?syn-25a6b1a6=1> spoke eloquently for his fellow former Barclays rates traders </news/barclays-traders-regret-not-helping-exonerated-colleagues-these-guys-were-our-friends> yesterday, as their criminal convictions for fixing the LIBOR market ten years ago were quashed.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It is maybe not quite as complete a vindication as he might have implied while hugging his lawyer – the Serious Fraud Office was keen to remind everyone that the reason for quashing the convictions was that there had been errors in the judge’s guidance ten years ago and that it’s not clear that they might not have been convicted anyway if that mistake had not been made. But be that as it may, the SFO seems to be of the view that it’s water under the bridge, the LIBOR market itself no longer exists and that consequently there’s no point in spending anyone’s time and money relitigating the 2010s. Barclays also decided not to make any comment.
All of which means that – since his case turns on exactly the same point of law – former Deutsche trader Christian Bittar </news/christian-bittar> will also soon be celebrating on the courtroom steps this Friday. Bittar was only second to Tom Hayes <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hayes_(trader)> himself in terms of his prominence in the LIBOR scandal – he famously made nearly EUR2bn in revenue for Deutsche Bank over a five year period, and received a $140m bonus in 2008. Bittar </news/christian-bittar> was sentenced to five years after pleading guilty in 2018, and has been appealing his conviction ever since the Supreme Court found that Hayes had been subject to a miscarriage of justice.
The question is, what next? Tom Hayes is currently suing his former employer, UBS, in the Connecticut courts, and the sums of money ($400m) involved are large even for someone like Bittar. The most recent filing in Hayes' case is a long memo <https://civilinquiry.jud.ct.gov/DocumentInquiry/DocumentInquiry.aspx?DocumentNo=33573635> from UBS setting out the case that co-operating with law enforcement is protected free speech, but if he’s in the mood for revenge, Bittar might do something similar.
Or he could get back into the market. With a quashed conviction, there’s nothing to stop Christian Bittar from returning to the financial services industry, and not so long ago there were hedge funds </news/barclays-traders-regret-not-helping-exonerated-colleagues-these-guys-were-our-friends>competing for his services. Bittar has a slight problem in that his experience as a short term interest futures trader might not be considered relevant given the substantial changes in market structure as a result of the LIBOR debacle. But he was genuinely regarded as a legend on the Deutsche trading desk, and there are plenty of his former colleagues who are still in the market and possibly able to vouch for him.
Alternatively, Bittar might choose to accept the clearing of his name, to be philosophical about the 23 months’ incarceration that he can’t get back, and get on with the rest of his life. After (presumably) opening a bottle of champagne and giving a short statement to the media, Christian Bittar will have a lot to think about this weekend.
Elsewhere, it’s not exactly “easy come, easy go”, but in the world of hedge funds it has to be some consolation while going through a period of bad returns to know that they are not (or at least, not yet) impairing your ability to raise funds. Hamza Lessougeur’s Arini Capital </news/barclays-traders-regret-not-helping-exonerated-colleagues-these-guys-were-our-friends>has had a tough time of it <https://www.ft.com/content/b52c8acc-7ea5-4bd0-b26a-b9956e19867b?syn-25a6b1a6=1> this year, with the flagship fund down 16%. But nonetheless, it’s raised $1.5bn <https://hedgeweek.com/news/arini-raises-1-5bn-for-credit-strategy-despite-flagship-fund-loss> in another fund.
This is partly because the fund that’s got the new money is Arini’s credit strategy, a highly concentrated fund which has been closed for years. Although 2026 has been a lousy environment for general credit investment, with situations like Altice and Aston Martin weighing on the market, it seems that investors still have confidence in Lessougeur.
It just goes to underline the wisdom of not always trying to maximise fee income. As well as keeping its size manageable so as not to drag on performance, closing the credit fund creates pent-up demand, and an investor base that will be prepared to subscribe even when others might be looking at the performance numbers and asking questions. Just like in show business, it’s best to leave them wanting more.
Meanwhile …
“I’m hopeful that it slows down and gets delayed … I’m not sure we’ve seen that much of it”. According to David Friedland of Citi, last year’s interruption in the poaching of junior staff by private equity has not continued into a trend. He also admitted that his 23 year-old son’s group chats had lit up this week with the big news </news/now-citi-will-promote-even-its-moderately-good-analysts-to-associate-after-two-years> about Citi’s graduate program. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-07/private-equity-isn-t-slowing-its-poaching-of-bankers-citi-executive-says?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261007&utm_campaign=author_21835441>)
Jane Dunlevie has been promoted from Chief Operating Officer of the TMT investment banking group at Goldman Sachs to be one of three co-heads with Jung Min and Barry O’Brien. (Finextra <https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48547/goldman-sachs-appoints-bankiong-tech-co-head>)
Stories of big team moves are always fascinating, and Gabriel Boghossian has been unusually open about how he organised his private equity secondaries legal team to go from Stephenson Harwood to A&O Sherman. Among the nuggets of information – they called it “Project Gunner” after their favourite football team, and they didn’t involve any headhunters because they were worried about conflicts of interest. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/project-gunner-how-a-o-shearman-hired-stephenson-harwoods-entire-secondaries-team-33a74908?mod=homepage>)
OpenAI have dropped the solutions to hundreds of previously unsolved mathematics problems on the internet. Mathematicians are worried about what this means for the future of the subject, and whether it will continue to be a good way to demonstrate one’s potential for making loads of money at a quant fund. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/openai-ai-math-problems-millennium-prize-23d14511?mod=mhp>)
Apparently people told Penny Pennington, the CEO of Edward Jones, that leaving a banking career to go into wealth management was “like jumping off a cliff”. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/edward-jones-ceo-leaving-banking-career-advice-2026-10>)
It’s not really a viable status symbol for a banker (unless they have a very large country house as well), but people are now prepared to pay up to $30,000 for an elite quality sheepdog. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-10-01/sheepdog-auction-in-skipton-sees-30-000-border-collies-sell-to-japan-us?srnd=homepage-uk>)

item.title: HRT hired Citadel's head of weather engineering in Chicago
item.description:
Two things are well known about Citadel. Firstly, it has one of the best weather forecasting teams in the hedge fund industry. Secondly, it has moved its head office from Chicago to Miami.
Now, one of its top weather forecasters in Chicago has moved to Hudson River Trading's (HRT) Chicago office.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Deron Roche, who joined Citadel in 2002 and was latterly titled 'Heather of Weather engineering, commodities, has moved to HRT as head of weather. Writing on LinkedIn, Roche said he'll be, "building at the intersection of weather, data, technology and markets."
Roche's departure from Citadel follows that of another Chicago-based weather-focused engineer, Alex Alifimoff. Alifimoff says on LinkedIn that he is now at Point72 in Connecticut, where he is 'head of AI weather."
Predicting the weather is an integral part of trading natural gas and commodities.
Citadel declined to comment. HRT didn't respond to a request to comment.

item.title: Barclays traders' regret at not helping pardoned colleagues: "These guys were our friends"
item.description:
As of today, the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/9c61d1a4-c982-41d5-a96e-f06df406c7e9?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reports that five Barclays traders sentenced to prison between 2016 and 2019 for manipulating interest rate benchmarks around a decade earlier, have had their convictions overturned.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
While the traders - Jonathan Mathew, Jay Merchant, Alex Pabon, Philippe Moryoussef and Colin Bermingham - will be celebrating tonight, colleagues who worked alongside them at Barclays are stricken with regret.
"The whole industry should be ashamed that this happened in the first place," says one senior trader who previously worked with some of those exonerated. "These guys were friends," he adds. "We were told by lawyers employed by the bank not to communicate with them."
Barclays declined to comment for this article. The five men were exonerated after it was accepted that the juries convicting them had been given the same inaccurate directions that juries had received in Tom Hayes' trial. These directions stated that if the individuals submitting the interest benchmarks took their own or the bank's commercial interests into account, then the submission was necessarily wrong or dishonest.
Hayes himself served five and a half years in prison </news/tom-hayes-carlo-palombo-supreme-court> and lost his marriage and health. His conviction was overturned last year and he is now suing UBS for $400m <https://www.ft.com/content/35bc9320-0232-4d9e-95f4-d81d2e36d6fd?syn-25a6b1a6=1> for malicious prosecution.
Hayes told us many of his former UBS colleagues reached out to him when he was released from prison in 2021, offering help. "Some said they felt sick that they hadn't helped when I needed it," he said. "The whole thing is hard - people needed to protect themselves. I get that they had careers and families."
Speaking to The Times <https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/barclays-traders-convictions-quashed-after-supreme-court-ruling-5lct0029g> 58-year old Moryoussef said, "for more than eight years, I have lived under the shadow of a conviction for something I did not do. I have lost my work, my career, my reputation and my income. I have been deprived of the chance to attend my beloved son’s graduation, to visit my dear mother and to make a pilgrimage to the grave of my late father.”
Hayes said it was a "fantastic day". "Sadly the UK remains an outlier in characterising industry practice as criminal. I hope that future appeals will clarify the position and the remaining convictions will be quashed."

item.title: Hedge fund Millennium ingested Jain Global's 2nd top marketing guy
item.description:
Jain Global is now running money exclusively for Millennium, but Jain Global is still its own place. As its own place, it still has its own very talented </news/jain-global-hedge-fund-costs> "35-year-old killer" </news/as-jain-global-p-ms-take-headhunter-calls-bobby-jain-explains-why-they-need-patience> portfolio managers, it still has its own communications team and it's still out there hiring new equities portfolio managers. </news/hedge-fund-jain-global-made-two-big-equities-hires-in-london>But it does not need anyone to raise external capital for a multistrategy hedge fund.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It is presumably with this in mind that Chris Mascarinas, Jain Global's managing director of marketing and investor relations, has appeared at Millennium in New York. There, Mascarinas has joined Millennium's capital development and investor relations team run by John Novogratz.
Novogratz has spent 17 years at Millennium. Mascarinas joined Jain Global in November 2023 and previously worked for six different funds, typically in investor relations roles. At least one member of his team has gone elsewhere: Emma Trenchard went to BDT & MSD Partners in September, for example.
Jain Global declined to comment. The chief marketing and investor relations officer at the fund has historically been Jaime Hobbeheydar; it's not clear whether he'll be going to Millennium too.
Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/jain-global-august-performance-returns-outside-money-millennium-2026-9> reported that Jain Global lost 0.2% in August, which was its last month managing money for outside investors. Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/jain-global-millennium-deal-details-equity-unit-exits-2026-5>also reported in May that Jain Global's back office staff had only been guaranteed compensation until December. It's not clear what happens next.
Writing in May, Business Insider also said that the future of Townie Wells, Jain Global's head of fundamental equities, was uncertain. However, Townie still appears to be there.
A handful of Jain Global portfolio managers have moved on. For example, Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/jain-global-head-of-equity-capital-markets-nitin-dewan-leaves-for-tudor-f06690bd>reported that Nitin Dewan, the co-head of US equity capital markets at Jain, joined Tudor as global head of ECM in September. Evan Fiedler, one of the earlier hires, appeared at DE Shaw in September. Sant Gupta </news/jain-global-s-singapore-senior-macro-pm-quietly-left-in-april-maybe-he-s-going-to-blue-crest> quietly left for BlueCrest in Singapore in April.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-01/jain-s-hedge-fund-made-1-8-billion-as-millennium-cash-rolls-in>reported last month that Jain Global has been marketing itself to talent as "a trading firm where portfolio managers collaborate with one another, whereas Millennium provides more independence and autonomy."
It's not clear whether portfolio managers at Jain Global will need to adhere to Millennium's strict approach to drawdowns, under which it's not uncommon for capital to be halved following a 5% loss and cut entirely </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-hedge-fund-millennium> following a loss of 7.5%. One source told us previously that Millennium often expects external funds it's invested in to adhere to these rules.

item.title: Hourly pay for technology jobs in finance is more than double what most engineers are earning
item.description:
Technology jobs in finance </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank> can be a bit gruelling </news/finance/problems-with-coding-jobs-in-banks> compared to other engineering roles, but the pay is often worth it. A new survey from Devographics, <https://2026.stateofdevs.com/en-US> State of Devs 2026, suggests financial services technologists earn much more than the rest.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The Devographics survey broke down average yearly compensation and average hours worked per week for technology professionals based on over 5,000 global responses. It found that tech staff on average work just under 40 hours per week, but also earn just $93k per year. Our 2026 Compensation Guide </news/finance-best-lifestyle> found that tech staff in finance make $264k on average at an average hourly pay of $116.
Where you work, of course, has a strong bearing on both hours and pay. Tech staff in France and the UK each work under 38 hours per week on average, but UK staff earn over $30k more per year. The Devographics survey found that engineers in the US and India </news/staff-in-goldman-sachs-low-cost-office-are-working-90-hour-weeks-too>worked the same number of hours on average, but American tech staff earned over four times the total annual compensation.
There are other curious differences between engineering jobs in different regions. The majority of respondents to the Devographics survey in India said they had just one computer monitor, whereas the majority of tech staff in the US and UK had two or more. US and UK engineers were equally likely to suffer from mental health issues, but US engineers were more likely to suffer from weight issues. UK staff also had a higher proportion of hybrid workers and a lower proportion of fully remote staff than the US.

item.title: HSBC hired hundreds of wealth managers in the UK. Now it may fire 70% of them
item.description:
Forget Jane Fraser and her aspiration to cut 20,000 jobs </news/citi-s-2026-layoffs-have-been-more-frequent-and-widespread-than-we-thought> at Citi, HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery is developing a strong reputation for being particularly willing to make hard decisions.
The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/dd553fc2-532c-4afc-a773-47cd7f786260?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported today that HSBC is planning "sweeping" cuts to its UK wealth business, which will result in 70% of its UK financial advisers being let go at the end of the month, following a mandatory consultation period.
A spokesperson for HSBC declared: “HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider. We’re continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally-enabled products and journeys, to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers.”
The cuts appear to have the blessing of Elhedery, who said <https://www.hsbc.com/news-and-views/views/hsbc-views/our-strategy-built-on-trust-accelerated-with-ai>this summer that HSBC is "empowering" its relationship managers with AI and reinvesting productivity gains. The AI empowerment is via a tool that "delivers real-time market insights and personalised investment strategies," said Elhedery.
In a possible leading indicator that something was afoot, Jose Carvalho, who arrived to run the UK wealth business in 2023, stepped down three weeks ago. Carvalho is now "rebalancing life and work" and the task of cutting 70% of the advisors will seemingly go to interim head Colin O'Flaherty, who wrote earlier this week that he feels "hugely privileged to lead the team."
HSBC insiders have been pointing out that it wasn't so long ago that HSBC was hiring hundreds of people in wealth management. In 2021, Nuno Matos, the former CEO of wealth and personal banking at HSBC, conceived a plan to add 5,000 "client-facing wealth planners" in Asia over a three to five year period. Matos left the bank last year and is now chief executive of ANZ. But Carvalho was overseeing an offshoot of Matos' plan in the UK and was said <https://www.theguardian.com/business/article/2024/sep/08/hsbc-on-hiring-spree-to-drive-uk-wealth-division-ambitions> to be preparing to hire "hundreds" of wealth managers across the country in 2025.
Many of those wealth managers were added around the country in places like Peterborough, Truro and Telford, where HSBC has offices. They were often relatively junior and moved into wealth management after starting their careers as cashiers or in mortgage advice.
It's not clear what they will do instead.
HSBC staff may be justified in feeling some trepidation about what will occur next. One insider told the FT the cuts are "brutal." Elhedery himself declared </news/hsbc-s-self-proclaimed-ruthless-ceo-is-not-its-most-feared-person>last year that he was prepared to be ruthless and to make difficult decisions.
Elhedery already closed HSBC's investment bank </news/hscb-closure-europe-us-job-cuts> (ex debt capital markets) outside of Asia and the Middle East. In March, Bloomberg reported </news/hsbc-ai-job-cuts> that HSBC was planning to use AI to replace 20,000 jobs in the next three to five years. CFO Manveen Kaur suggested jobs requiring "very basic binary decision making" were being automated, but said that at Hang Seng bank in Asia at least, HSBC would be "upskilling" its people rather than cutting jobs. In the UK, this doesn't appear to be so.

item.title: One of HSBC's top FX traders escaped to Citadel
item.description:
HSBC may have cut a lot of its London investment bankers. It may have cut a lot of its London equity researchers and traders. But it is still a big trader of FX for its corporate clients. Nonetheless, one of its London FX managing directors (MDs) has left it.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Vineet Mudgil, an MD in FX options trading who had hitherto been loyal to HSBC since joining the bank in Mumbai in 2008 and moving to London in 2011, has left the bank. He has gone to Citadel to become a portfolio manager instead.
HSBC didn't respond to a request to comment on Mudgil's departure. Nor did Mudgil himself. Nor did Citadel. Mudgil has announced his whereabouts on LinkedIn. The FCA Register says he left HSBC in April, suggesting he's spent the past six months on gardening leave.
There were suggestions <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/hsbc-mulls-outsourcing-some-fixed-income-trading-bloomberg-news-reports-2025-03-24/>in March 2025 that HSBC was considering outsourcing some fixed income trading to Citadel Securities, but HSBC subsequently denied this. <https://www.ifre.com/bonds/2019087/hsbc-must-shield-fx-cash-cow-from-any-citadel-securities-or-jane-street-tie-up>
HSBC has stopped splitting out revenues for its equities and its fixed income traders, but in the first six months of this year, revenues in the combined business increased by a mere 2%. FX revenues, however, contributed to an overall 5% increase in transaction banking revenues in the corporate and institutional bank in the first half.
One headhunter said Mudgil is a "decent trader." Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-01/hsbc-s-new-city-trading-floor-is-far-shorter-than-banking-rivals>reported last week that HSBC's new trading floor will have unusually low ceilings; Mudgil will not need to experience this.

item.title: Inside Eisler Capital's last year: Plastic bottle recycling, weekly risk meetings, $1.5m pay
item.description:
Hedge fund Eisler Capital is no longer managing money, but it is still filing accounts. Accounts for the final year of Eisler Capital Management Ltd. and its subsidiary Eisler Capital (HC) Ltd. offer some final fleeting insights into what it was like to work there.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
There was some keen recycling going on. Eisler had a program for reusable water bottles and had banned the use of single use plastic bottles on its premises. There were also a lot of meetings: Eisler's management committee and risk management committee would convene once a week; its valuation committee and operational risk committee would meet once a month; its conflicts committee would meet once a quarter.
Despite all the meetings and recycling, Eisler announced it would wind down its multistrategy fund in September 2025, redeemed its own investments in the fund by December, and moved out of its offices.
The filings also show Eisler's deteriorating profitability. In its final year of operation, operating profit fell 65% and the firm made a $7.5m loss after tax.
Declining operating profits were partly the result of rising pay. Total compensation spending for Eisler's 296 employees rose 24% to consume 83% of revenues. Average pay per employee went from $1.1m to $1.5m, probably including spending on severance.
It's tempting to think that tax charges tipped Eisler over the edge. Instead, it seems that winding down the fund meant R&D tax credits had to be written off, resulting in the $15.9m charge.
Amidst all this, Eisler's directors and shareholders were hit hardest. The unnamed highest paid director took a 70% pay cut, but still received $1.7m. Dividends fell 73%, but were still $11.6m and used to offset a loan made by Eisler's UK subsidiary to its parent company in the Cayman Islands.

item.title: As HSBC cuts private bankers in London, an MD in Asia walked away
item.description:
It's a tense moment to be a private banker </news/private-banking-jobs-vs-investment-banking-jobs> at HSBC in London. The FT <https://www.ft.com/content/dd553fc2-532c-4afc-a773-47cd7f786260?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported today that close to 70% of financial advisers in the bank's UK wealth business could be cut by the end of the month as part of the bank's ongoing AI transformation </news/hsbc-ai-job-cuts>. At the same time, one of the bank's most senior private bankers in Asia has separately departed.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Catherine Claire Lim, an MD and desk head for China and Hong Kong, departed the bank last week according to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) register. She announced via LinkedIn that she is joining Singaporean bank DBS as its market head for North Asia.
Lim spent the last four years at HSBC. Before that, she worked in the private banking arms of several top banks in Asia. She was a director at Citi and Standard Chartered, and an executive director at UBS. She began her career in banking as an executive assistant in the consumer finance division of Singaporean bank OCBC before becoming a relationship manager.
HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery said in a July report <https://www.privatebanking.hsbc.com/media-releases-and-news/ida-liu-appointed-ceo-hsbc-private-bank/> that the bank is "empowering relationship managers with AI" to personalize experiences for customers. It's hiring "at least 100 AI specialists" in a new Singapore AI centre of excellence to facilitate this. However, headhunters told us last year </news/this-is-what-your-private-banking-salary-and-bonus-should-be-in-singapore> relationship managers aren't being replaced in Asia because "the higher echelon clients still have an appreciation for private bankers." HSBC itself has made several senior hires <https://asianbankingandfinance.net/wealth-management/news/hsbc-private-bank-makes-four-senior-hires-across-asia> in Asia this year, including new desk heads for global India, offshore China and Singapore.

item.title: Morning Coffee: It’s a bad year for bonuses to be so big anyway. How to dress for your high profile hedge fund divorce
item.description:
It seems the investment banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> industry has forgotten that proverb about counting one’s chickens before they’ve hatched. Already, less than two weeks into the last quarter, we are all talking about record-breaking bonuses <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-06/wall-street-eyes-record-bonuses-as-profit-heads-past-90-billion>. After all, it’s not as if anything bad has ever happened to spoil the party in October <https://www.investopedia.com/articles/financial-theory/09/october-effect.asp>, is it?
Even given the extremely strong performance of revenues for the year to date, and the fact that Q4 is traditionally the smallest contributor to the year’s earnings, we’d guess that top management will react to adverse events in the fourth quarter by engaging in some serious “expectations management”. It’s never healthy for bankers to be doing victory laps and acting like everything’s fantastic.
For one thing, it’s not necessarily a good time to have noticeable deep pockets, given the fiscal environment in a number of the world's largest financial centres. Several finance ministries are quite pointedly refusing to rule out <https://www.ft.com/content/3cd5097b-b5ca-4b9f-83fd-f008bb2b72d3?syn-25a6b1a6=1> special banking taxes, even if Jamie Dimon thinks they’re unfair <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-06/dimon-says-a-uk-windfall-tax-on-domestic-banks-wouldn-t-be-fair?srnd=homepage-uk>. The political climate isn’t quite as hostile to bankers as it used to be – data centres and techbros have taken over as the main folk villains, but an article on bonuses in the Guardian <https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/27/londons-investment-bankers-lawyers-paid-more-than-1bn> last week is a reminder that hostility hasn't gone away. It seems foolhardy to talk too much about record bonuses, and remind the voters why they used to hate us.
You are also only as good as your last couple of trades. (On Wall Street, that is; in Silicon Valley venture capital you can spend your whole career talking about having been an early investor in Paypal or Facebook). Big IPOs are getting postponed <https://www.wsj.com/finance/stocks/what-ouras-stalled-ipo-tells-us-about-one-hit-wonders-31921bf5?st=8SHQQi&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink> and cancelled, bond yields are moving upward, and although the bull market is presently still charging, it would be a brave forecaster who claimed to be totally confident that things will be just as great or better twelve months from now.
Most bankers’ compensation packages contain a significant deferred component, much of which is tied to the stock price. This gets more true the further up the hierarchy you go. For bankers of Executive Director </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>rank or above, the difference between a great and a mediocre year for the bonus </news/banking-bonuses-london>pool can easily be outweighed by the difference between getting your equity-comp at an all-time low or an all-time high price. Consider Deutsche Bank employees, who had a quite miserable compensation round in 2021 <https://www.google.com/search?q=2021+efinancialcareers+deutsche+bank%23&oq=2021+efinancialcareers+deutsche+bank%23&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOdIBCDU4OTlqMGo5qAIAsAIB&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8>, but who might view it considerably more happily now that it turns out that long-term deferred equity from that year has gone up by nearly three times.
One thing which is likely to make the 2026 bonus round a bit nicer is that, for the first time in a while, there should at least be enough for everyone to get treated fairly. There won’t need to be any aggravating arguments about divisions between traders and bankers, and there’s no need to concentrate rewards on rainmakers; the poor old infantry who execute the transactions are just as necessary in conditions like this. The labour market is reasonably tight, and so there are good grounds for everyone to feel happy about their jobs. There’s just no need to shout about it.
Elsewhere, if you’re ever in the position of fighting a court case over the valuation of one of the world’s biggest quant funds, don’t forget your “red glasses <https://nypost.com/2026/10/06/us-news/billionaire-in-njs-biggest-divorce-case-wins-bid-to-protect-hedge-fund-secrets-from-going-public/>, a cream blazer, blue plaid pants and gun-metal-colored woven leather heeled mules”. Or possibly “a gray-and-white striped jacket <https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/inside-the-n-j-courtroom-where-a-hedge-fund-titans-messy-divorce-is-playing-out-b9e3ce32>, white slacks and chunky blue heels”. If you’re a man, the look is apparently “navy-blue suit, light blue shirt and no tie”, although we’d guess you could get away with a Patagonia fleece vest if you went to court straight from the office.
It seems that one of the reasons that the finance press have decided to go all Fashion Week in describing John and Laura Overdeck’s outfits, as they cover the TwoSigma co-founder’s divorce case is that they’ve not got much else to write about. John Overdeck’s lawyers are trying to keep as many financial details out of the public filings as possible, in order to avoid revealing company secrets. Since one of the most important matters at issue is the actual value of the company – the two sides disagree by a factor of 50% on what the Overdeck stake is worth – this means that so far it’s purely a human interest story.
Meanwhile …
The promise of AI was that it could give every employee a dozen assistants. The reality of AI is that every employee feels like they’re now responsible for managing a dozen assistants. And this apparently involves carrying out constant performance reviews and improvement plans on the ones that aren’t working out. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/ai-agents-managing-more-annoying-managing-people-2026-10>)
John Torgeby, the CEO of Sweden’s largest bank SEB, has resigned very suddenly indeed. It is apparently for personal and family reasons; analysts and investors seem to be saying that they are taking the company statement at face value. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-06/seb-ceo-torgeby-resigns-from-swedish-bank-for-personal-reasons>)
Alternative careers for bankers – if you are already used to poor sleep, stress and constantly changing requirements, you can apparently earn $100,000 a trip by steering a boat through the Strait of Hormuz. If you’re not currently qualified to captain an oil tanker, there are apparently pretty good danger bonuses for crew as well. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/0d665e5b-d8c8-4f1e-acf5-bba7193b4e6e?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Brevan Howard is not necessarily like other multi-strats; its top managers, including Fash Golchin, can be given proportionately very large allocations of its master fund’s capital. (Navnoor Bawa Resarch <https://www.navnoorbawaresearch.com/p/brevan-howards-flagship-is-not-a?utm_source=substack&publication_id=5040435&post_id=219007390&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=qrn8&triedRedirect=true>)
The Piper Sandler / Perella Weinberg deal might have kicked off a round of consolidation among the boutique investment bank sector. (Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/boutique-investment-banks-look-to-m-a-in-race-to-add-scale-8bf38fa2?mod=topic_news>)
As Paul Tudor Jones put it, “If I think about the end of my life and I look back, I’m not gonna be thinking about the ’87 crash or Bitcoin. I’m gonna be thinking about who I loved and who loved me” (Of Dollars and Data <https://ofdollarsanddata.com/playing-the-wrong-game/>)
Obviously, Warren Buffett has more than earned the right to spend his retirement any way he likes, but there is something a little disappointing about learning that he mainly hangs around watching YouTube clips. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/warren-buffett-youtube-watching-cb6bd1d4?mod=mhp>)

item.title: Tragic death of JPMorgan trader on charity bike ride
item.description:
A 500-mile charity bike ride last week ended in tragedy after one of the participants died suddenly on the first day.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Tributes have been made to Dan Singer, a 48-year-old European commercial bond trader at JPMorgan, who died during the ride last Thursday. His cause of death has not been confirmed.
Singer was a former player at Rosslyn Park FC in West London. He and 11 former teammates were riding to raise money for The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity and The Brain Tumour Charity, via the Lewis Moody Foundation, in support of Crawford Henderson, a former teammate battling a brain tumour.
Writing on its website <https://rosslynpark.co.uk/club-statement-remembering-dan-singer/>, Rosslyn Park said Singer was a "much-loved friend."
Donations for the ride <https://givestar.io/team/rfc500> have so far raised nearly £66k and are now being made in memory of Singer as well as for Henderson. Others on the ride included Des Anderson, managing partner at hedge fund Marshall Wace.
The 500-mile journey was intended to take place over six days and to match Henderson's journey from Strone in Scotland, via Durham and Oxford Universities, and on to London. Writing on LinkedIn before setting off from Strone on Thursday, Singer said "I am not a cyclist" but that it was a great privilege to be joining the ride for Crawford.
Singer joined JPMorgan from Morgan Stanley in 2013. Tributes to him on Instagram said he was "much loved" and an "amazing man."
The rest of the ride was cancelled after Singer's death. A short ride to Rosslyn Park took place in his memory last Saturday, followed by the planned lunch and fundraising. "Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Dan's wife Michelle, his family and friends, and all those who were riding alongside him," said Rosslyn Park president Adam Tyrer. A minute's silence was held before Rosslyn Park's game against Sheffield.

item.title: Balyasny hired the former head of Citadel's data strategies group
item.description:
As we've previously noted, data specialists </news/data-strategist-hedge-fund>are in high demand among hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> and trading firms. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> Balyasny </news/where-do-portfolio-managers-work-balyasny>is no exception; it just hired a quant </news/quant-jobs-finance>who previously led one of Citadel's data analysis teams.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Halla Yang joined the hedge fund this month as a senior quant researcher based in Chicago. He was at Citadel for eight years, spending five of them as co-head (then sole head) of its data strategies group. Citadel's website <https://www.citadel.com/careers/career-perspectives/real-people-real-impact-how-alternative-data-powers-investment-decisions-at-citadel/> says this team "focus[es] exclusively on alternative data rather than traditional market data;" it uses AI </news/how-hedge-funds-use-ai> to analyze messy data like satellite imagery, providing analysis to the fund's investment teams. Yang left Citadel in April 2025 and appears to have been sitting out a non-compete prior to joining Balyasny.
Before Citadel, Yang worked across a variety of companies. He was a data scientist at McKinsey, a quant researcher at Jump Trading and a VP at Goldman Sachs. Yang is also a competitions grandmaster on competitive data analysis platform Kaggle </news/how-to-get-a-quant-research-job-in-a-hedge-fund#:~:text=The%20quant%20also%20said%20that%20competitions%20on%20data%20science%20platform%20Kaggle%20are%20also%20highly%20regarded.%C2%A0>; there are just 407 of these in the world.
Obtaining insights from unusual data sources can be trickier than it sounds. Earlier this year, a member of Jane Street's alternative data team said </news/one-of-jane-street-s-most-important-teams-is-full-of-professional-speed-daters> that satellite imagery of Walmart parking lots, the most famous alt data example, is "really indirect," showing you only how many people showed up rather than how much they're spending.
In London, Balyasny added to its tech team by hiring Chris Norman to work on systematic infrastructure. He spent the last eight years in crypto; he was head engineering at crypto trading firm GSR and a tech lead at crypto exchange Blockchain.com. Before that, Norman was a team lead at Sun Trading, the electronic market maker acquired by Hudson River Trading in 2018.

item.title: Are these the only portfolio managers doing well during a brutal month for macro?
item.description:
It's been a brutal few weeks for macro hedge fund </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund>managers of the world. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-02/hedge-funds-exiting-crowded-trades-fueled-rout-in-french-bonds>reported last Friday that after losing money in mid-September following the Federal Reserve's first rate increase since 2023, macro funds lost money again last week after carry trades relating to French bonds blew up.
There is blood on the carpet. Some of the best known portfolio managers </news/2023/09/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund> at some of the biggest funds are thought to be nursing large losses. None of the funds concerned have confirmed this. Only the unfortunate macro-focused Taula Capital Management </news/diego-megia-taula-capital>is known to have been down 9.4% in September <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/hedge-fund-taula-down-9-4-in-volatile-year-for-macro-traders>.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Even Taula, though, is understood to have portfolio managers who are doing well. There are unconfirmed suggestions that Lewis Morton, the former star portfolio manager at Eisler Capital, is up nearly $20m this year and that Josh Blakely, who came from Millennium, is also doing fine.
Similarly, it's suggested that James Watson, </news/now-hedge-fund-balyasny-hired-barclays-head-of-euro-swaps-trading> formerly of Millennium is personally doing well at Balyasny </news/balyasny-hedge-fund> Asset Management, even though Bloomberg said BAM lost money on the French trade. Ex-Goldman Sachs managing director and rates trader Andrew Bound </news/hedge-fund-citadel-london-partners> is said to be up at Citadel. This is unconfirmed by either the individuals or the firms concerned, though.
More broadly, it's thought that many macro teams are nursing large losses that they are unlikely to recover from this year. This is problematic because such portfolio managers become "zombies." </news/millennium-hedge-fund-jobs>Losses are typically carried forward to the next year and must be recovered before bonuses are paid. At firms like Millennium, salaries may also be treated as an advance against future profits.
This is why a period of deep losses is often followed by a rush to join new funds with a clean slate. Excepting the names above, we could therefore be in for a period of high PM liquidity in London.
Or not. The head of one pod said many people are getting tapped on the shoulder. "But the problem with a year like this is that with lots of PMs down, you fire one and hire another guy who lost money as well."

item.title: What you need to know about fintech stock pay today: "Everything is up for discussion"
item.description:
The greatest appeal of joining a budding start-up </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-fintech>is often equity pay </news/how-much-do-fintech-startup-jobs-really-pay>, with lucrative upside if the company grows to be worth billions of dollars. Today, as valuations in major AI labs </news/the-difference-between-working-as-a-quant-in-finance-and-as-a-researcher-in-an-ai-lab>balloon and quant firms </news/pay-for-electronic-trading-graduates-is-soaring-1m-at-hrt-850k-at-jane-street>offer $1m compensation packages right out of the gate, the risks of joining a start-up are starting to seem much greater than the rewards. Industry experts speaking at the Sifted Summit last week have described how companies are changing their approach to equity compensation in order to fight back.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
"This is not a playbook era," said Michelle Coventry, VP of talent for VC fund Creandum. "Anything to do with equity compensation is up for discussion." Four-year vesting periods, </news/fintech-culture-and-stock-pay> which have historically been popular, aren't viable for certain roles where the average tenure is falling; Coventry said that top go-to-market professionals now stay at start-ups for just "24 to 26 months" on average. She said that start-ups are having to take "creative approaches" to accommodate these hires because "everyone wants something different."
The nature of exit opportunities has changed too. Katie Conn, an investment manager for VC firm </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-venture-capital>Salica Investments, said that the "IPO market </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> has been fairly quiet and M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma>hasn't filled that gap." This is not always due to a lack of success in the businesses; Mike Turner, partner in the M&A practice of Latham & Watkins, said that "companies are able to stay private for longer and choosing to [do so]," due to an abundance of late-stage growth capital.
To keep employees engaged, and to give them an opportunity to cash out stock, secondary share sales have exploded in popularity over the past few years. These used to be frowned upon, as they signalled you weren't close to an exit; Coventry said that "secondaries used to be a dirty word," while Crowdcube CEO Matt Cooper said that conversations on secondaries used to happen in "dark rooms with hushed tones." Today, they have become a status symbol of the fastest-rising start-ups, and a chance to update your firm's valuation.
Fintechs have been at the forefront of this. Revolut has more than doubled its valuation <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/revoluts-rise-become-europes-115-billion-big-bank-rival-2026-10-04/> in the past two years using secondary sales. Stripe's valuation was cut in half to $50bn <https://www.reuters.com/technology/fintech-stripe-valued-50-bln-after-65-bln-fundraise-2023-03-15/> during its last primary fundraising round in 2023, but it achieved a valuation of $159bn <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/24/stripe-value-stock-sale-tender-offer.html> during a secondary share sale this February.
Employees don't reap the maximum benefit from these share sales. Manish Prayaga, founder of cap table management platform Terraledge, told us that employees often sell their shares "at quite a steep discount on the headline valuation for that company" during a secondaries transaction. The discount can be as much as 30 to 50 percent.
The discount isn't as steep for established companies; Prayaga said that, "obviously, a series B company is higher risk than Anthropic, which is much later stage, so the level of discount is proportional to that." He said that secondary sales are still very attractive to startup employees because you can wait "for an exit event which might take a couple more years… or you could use that money to put a deposit down on a house.”
You might even get a better deal than you would if you wait for an IPO. One fintech startup founder, speaking to us anonymously, said "there's a huge bubble in private markets right now versus public... the money is just flowing right now and I think a lot of startups are exploiting it." Private markets dictate valuations up to the point of an IPO, but then employees with stock have to wait out an excruciating six-month lockup period. </news/ex-barclays-and-morgan-stanley-bankers-holding-millions-at-figma-face-an-awkward-5-months>

item.title: Morning Coffee: How Citi is managing the most awkward bit of its new analyst program. The new technology interviews
item.description:
As we noted yesterday </news/now-citi-will-promote-even-its-moderately-good-analysts-to-associate-after-two-years>, Citi has begun promoting its analysts to associates in two years instead of three. Citi was promoting some analysts to associates in two years previously, but only the very best ones. Now, everyone will be expedited. Good times indeed!
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Unless, of course, you're a current third year Citi analyst, about to become an associate, in which case you might look askance at the newly promoted associates with up to a third less experience than you and wonder whether their AI prompting skills are really sufficient to close the gap.
Citi appears to have thought of this issue. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-05/citi-speeds-junior-bankers-ascent-in-fight-with-private-equity>reported yesterday that Citi's current third year analysts will be promoted to associate as usual on January 1st. By comparison, the second year analysts who are being promoted early to associates will probably not get the call until around July 2027.
In this way, the current third years will get a whole year of associate salaries and associate bonuses, whereas the expedited second years will only get six months. Effectively, they are being promoted six months early.
Bloomberg says the move is to stop Citi's juniors leaving for the likes of private equity, but some senior Citi insiders say there's been a constant dribbling out of analysts and associates this year that needed to be stemmed. Shortening the analyst program could help, although Bloomberg notes that January's associate promotions will be 'subject to performance,' implying that nothing is guaranteed.
Separately, TechCrunch <https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/05/hackerranks-ai-interviewer-offers-a-glimpse-into-what-job-interviews-could-become/?utm_medium=organic_social&utm_source=TWITTER> reports that HackerRank </news/2020/12/coding-interviews-hackerrank-nightmare>, the coding test company that has long been the bane of anyone attempting to get a technology job in banking has developed a new product called Chakra.
This does not refer to a crystal with the ability to solve the Trapping Rain Water Problem </news/2023/02/goldman-sachs-leetcode-problem>, but to a new and dynamic system in which you work through a coding task using a code repository and an AI assistant ("Chakra") that keeps asking what you're doing and introducing new constraints. Sounds great.
Meanwhile...
Citi will also end its fixed-term employment provision that typically applied to investment banking analysts in North America, meaning those employees no longer have a pre-determined contractual end date. (Financial Times) < https://www.ft.com/content/41b567dc-50e9-4c41-95bb-e295caaf2340?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Citi is now the top underwriter for IPOs globally (based on the first nine months of the year). Vis Raghavan will be proud. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-06/citi-takes-top-spot-in-global-ipo-underwriting-through-september?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261006&utm_campaign=author_16891741>
Dwayne Lysaght says JPMorgan has a "growth mindset" in European investment banking. “We want to instil the mentality that you should not be content to win the race by one second, but by a distance,” said his co-head, Alberto Piana. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/jpmorgans-new-european-dealmaking-bosses-we-want-to-win-by-a-distance-e4a12948>
Global M&A revenues also appear to be slowing down. They were $1.7t in Q2 and $986bn in Q3. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/00fb4438-1f86-4bf2-a165-0c39f3fd506b?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
TRex Bio Inc., an early-stage biotech focused on autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, wants to raise up to $133.3m in an IPO. JPMorgan, Evercore, Cantor Fitzgerald, Stifel and Wedbush PacGrow are working on it. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-05/eli-lilly-backed-trex-bio-seeks-to-raise-133-3-million-in-ipo?taid=6ac3c729b459b60001b7f9e6&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
A woman who became a JPMorgan MD aged 29 is selling her $37bn Palmer Square CLO business </news/jp-morgan-md-29> to Goldman Sachs for an unspecified price, and now everyone wants to buy a CLO business for the lucrative flow of fees from deals already created. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-05/goldman-s-bid-for-clo-manager-highlights-wall-street-s-fee-hunt?taid=6ac3bdc9c39c650001a4dea6&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>)
Three years ago, Dmitry Balyasny took over Balyasny's equities business. Now things have been shaken up and star Balyasny stock picker Ilan Weiss has been promoted to co-head of equities alongside him. Weiss's team has generated the highest profits in the equities business. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-05/balyasny-elevates-star-stock-picker-weiss-to-co-lead-equities?taid=6ac3cbdab459b60001b7fa3f&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Hedge funds like Taula and Balyasny had piled into carry trades to profit from the difference between interest-rate swaps and French yields. They had to unwind these quickly last Thursday when French bonds slumped. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-02/hedge-funds-exiting-crowded-trades-fueled-rout-in-french-bonds>
Critical things to consider when you're writing your CV now. What is the hardest-to-fake evidence that you are good? What have you built or done that gives the interviewer something concrete to ask about? (YoungandCalculated) <https://youngandcalculated.substack.com/p/the-quant-resume-that-actually-gets?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=4607221&post_id=218931493&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=k3np9&triedRedirect=true&utm_medium=email>
A retired City lawyer, who lives in Wandsworth, south London paid £2k in council tax last year. In April 2028 his bills will rise to almost £9k. "I’ve paid my taxes all my working life, and hoped that my savings could benefit my five children and grandchildren.” (The Times) <https://www.thetimes.com/money/tax/article/my-tax-bill-will-go-up-7000-the-london-borough-facing-record-rises-8x6zgwxps>
Mamdani: “Socialism to me means you’ll have whatever you need to live a dignified life and that it is the government’s job to deliver on that.... When people say dignity we’re talking about the things that allow you to take a breath. Housing, child care, public transit. No one should be priced out of these things. These are nonnegotiables, you need these to live.” (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/opinion/free-expression/under-socialism-dignity-is-an-impossible-dream-4e47a4fb?mod=e2tw>

item.title: Hudson River Trading hired an executive from an eco-friendly high-performance computing firm
item.description:
Will the battle for alpha among quant traders </news/quant-jobs-finance> be decided by whoever has the best data centre? Hedge funds and algorithmic trading firms alike </news/data-centres-hedge-funds>are hiring hardware specialists just in case. At Hudson River Trading, </news/the-coffee-run-the-kind-trading-firm-paying-1m-to-graduates-and-100m-to-its-top-people>which has been known to let its traders spend up to $1k a day on tokens </news/ai-token-use-traders>, the latest arrival in this space is a former executive of a publicly traded high-performance computing firm.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
HRT hired Harry McHugh as a systems engineer, based in Singapore according to his LinkedIn profile. He spent the last two years as chief information officer of DUG, an Australian technology firm that provides cloud-based high-performance computing services similar to those on offer by 'neoclouds' like CoreWeave. DUG touts a proprietary immersion cooling system <https://dug.com/dug-cool/> that can cut data centre water usage by up to 25%.
McHugh also spent three and a half years with hardware manufacturer AMD, where he was a senior member of technical staff working on semiconductors. He joined after a previous stint at DUG, where he was head of high-performance computing.
He'll have his work cut out for him at Hudson River Trading which, like most quant firms, has been building a colossal hardware stack. The firm has stated in job listings that it has "triple-digit petabyte-scale storage and massive CPU and GPU clusters </news/programming-languages-machine-learning-ai-quant> in globally distributed data centers." In its UK entity, HRT spent £2.4m per head </news/hudson-river-trading-pay-uk-high-frequency-trading>on new equipment last year, roughly triple its spending on compensation. In August, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-20/hudson-river-signs-multibillion-dollar-coreweave-crwv-deal-for-ai-cloud>reported that it also entered a multi-billion-dollar agreement with neocloud provider CoreWeave.
Elsewhere in Asia, Goldman Sachs has been bolstering its own electronic trading division. It hired Ross Whittaker as an MD and head of APAC algo trading. He was previously head of pan-Asian electronic execution at Citi, but left in July. </news/another-electronic-equities-md-exited-citi>

item.title: Multiple portfolio managers said to be leaving BlueCrest, including 26-year-old star
item.description:
It's been a difficult year for macro hedge funds </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund>, and a particularly difficult September. Against this backdrop, various portfolio managers appear to have left BlueCrest Capital Management, for reasons that are unclear.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
BlueCrest didn't respond to multiple requests to comment for this article. Nor did the portfolio managers concerned, but we understand that around 10 people have either left recently or are leaving.
The departures are thought to include Ben Turner, the 26 year-old ex-Barclays </news/barclays-macro-to-hedge-funds>sterling rates trader who became a BlueCrest partner on May 1st </news/ben-turner-bluecrest>. Turner is still registered at BlueCrest with the FCA, however. The FCA Register shows Robert Robinson, who joined from Hudson River Trading, leaving the UK entity on September 25th. Others, like Tom Bowden (now at Wellington) and Ankur Aneja </news/bluecrest-hiring-traders-from-banks>left earlier this year. Ben Atlas left and went to ExodusPoint.
The departures from BlueCrest may be partly voluntary, but come after top macro portfolio managers at multiple major funds are thought to have had a challenging September. This includes, but is by no means limited to, Taula Capital Management. </news/diego-megia-taula-capital>
BlueCrest had 46 London partners last time it filed accounts. It paid them an average of £959k each in the year to March 2025. </news/bluecrest-london-pay>
Many of those leaving are thought to have come from BlueCrest's rates trading business, which is run by Joseph Walkrush from Miami.

item.title: Now Citi will promote even its moderately good analysts to associate after two years
item.description:
How long will it take you to progress from analyst to associate </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds>in an investment banking </news/what-is-an-investment-bank> team? This depends upon how good you are and where you work.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
If you work for Citi, you will now be lucky indeed. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-05/citi-speeds-junior-bankers-ascent-in-fight-with-private-equity?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261005&utm_campaign=author_21835441>reports that Citi is shortening the length of its analyst program to two years, after which all analysts will be transformed into beautiful associates.
Bloomberg says Citi's analyst program previously ran for three years. David Friedland, co-head of North America investment banking, told Bloombeg the truncation of the three year program will bring Citi in line with some competitors. It will also enable Citi analysts to earn higher pay, sooner. Bloomberg suggests the change will discourage these analysts from leaving for private equity and notes that it will now be possible to go from analyst to vice president (VP) at Citi within the blink of five and a half years.
All of this sounds appealing, but it's also worth noting that none of this is entirely new. We reported in 2019 </news/2019/03/analyst-to-associate-to-vp-investment-banks>that Citi, UBS, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were promoting analysts to associates after two years. At that point they'd already been doing it for a while. Goldman Sachs, for example, began promoting analysts to associate in 2016. </news/2016/08/goldman-sachs-early-associate-promotions>
So what's new? Citi declined to comment, but we understand from senior insiders at the bank that the key change is the breadth of the two year program at Citi. Previously, only the very best analysts were promoted to associate after two years. Now, it seems that all Citi analysts will be.
UBS is thought to have a similar approach. So is Goldman Sachs. </news/2021/05/ubs-associate-bonus>
First year analysts at all banks earn around $160k in total compensation. </news/banking-pay>Third year analysts earn around $200k. However, first year associates earn around $276k, so Citi's third year analysts may effectively receive a $76k pay rise.
Curiously, the promotions come at a moment in time when private equity firms are struggling to exit investments, suggesting competition for junior talent may be less fierce than in the past. They also come as AI is being used to do the jobs of junior bankers </news/ai-in-ma-banking>, suggesting that fewer and higher calibre juniors may be the way forward.

item.title: Citi hired a new chief technology officer from UBS
item.description:
Citi's CTO David Griffiths </news/citi-s-cto-says-these-are-the-kinds-of-jobs-he-s-eliminating-with-ai> had a change of role this summer, becoming the bank's group head of artificial intelligence. </news/citi-s-ai-driven-productivity-boom-spells-hard-times-for-banking-contractors>The bank has now appointed his successor, and he comes from UBS.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Paul McEwen joined Citi as chief technology </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank> officer and head of infrastructure, based in New York. He spent the last 12 and a half years at UBS in a variety of senior roles including global head of technology services, as well as group head of infrastructure and security engineering. In the middle of that stint, he left for Wells Fargo, where he worked for seven months as its head of infrastructure before returning to UBS.
McEwan is a citi alum. He was at the bank from 2000 to 2006 and served as global head of applications. He also spent eight years at JPMorgan where he was CTO of client services.
As head of infrastructure, McEwen will presumably work alongside Griffiths on Arc, Citi's internal agentic platform <https://time.com/collection/executives-of-the-year-tech-data/2026/david-griffiths/#:~:text=Arc%2C%20Citi%E2%80%99s%20internal,bank%2C%E2%80%9D%20Griffiths%20says.> which launched earlier this year. McEwen wrote in an article earlier this year that UBS has been working on AI agents too and is "seeing promising results... in areas such as triaging security alerts, clearing tickets that pile up, and creating incident closure summaries." UBS and Citi declined to comment.
UBS isn't the only European bank that lost a senior technologist to an American bank this month. Li Yang, global head of structured products technology for Barclays, left to join Wells Fargo, where he will work as head of structured derivatives technology.

item.title: Citadel Securities rescued a dispossessed marketer for its equity sales team
item.description:
To paraphrase Rhett Butler in Gone with the Wind, there is more good hiring to be done when a hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> fails than when one succeeds. The latest blockade runner, on the buy-side at least, is Citadel Securities.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Brant Duber joined Citadel Securities’ franchise sales team in New York two weeks ago. Duber joined the firm from hedge fund Eminence Capital </news/2023/03/goldman-sachs-program-trading>, the $7bn hedge fund founded and run by Ricky Sandler, where he was director of marketing. Eminence Capital was wound up earlier this year by Sandler due to a sustained period of “underperformance and rising structural challenges”, Business Times reported <https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/companies-markets/banking-finance/ricky-sandler-shuttering-eminence-capital-after-27-year-run>.
Before Eminence Capital, which he joined in 2023, Duber spent 15 years in Goldman Sachs’ equities team. He was made a managing director in its class of 2021 promotions </news/2021/11/goldman-sachs-mds-2021>.
Eminence Capital’s former employees have been dispersed into many corners of the financial services industry. Luke Brzozowski, for example, was a consumer staples portfolio manager at the firm; he’s since gone to Rokos. Nicholas Freymuth, a quantitative developer at the defunct firm, became CTO of $35bn long-only fund Eagle Capital Management.
As far as we can tell, Duber is the only one who has left for Citadel or Citadel Securities. Neither he nor Citadel Securities responded to a request for comment.
